a-dictid="0539eefe3f169277718547881d187d">crescent in shape

Explanation:

The right adrenal gland is triangular or pyramidal, not crescent-shaped.

Right Adrenal Gland

  • Shape: Pyramidal
  • Parts:
    • Base: Below, overlaps the upper end of the right kidney.
    • Apex: Above, anterior surface presents a hilum.
    • Anterior Surface:
      • Medial area: Related to the inferior vena cava (IVC).
      • Lateral area: Related to the liver.
    • Posterior Surface:
      • Upper area: Related to the diaphragm.
      • Lower area: Related to the kidney.
    • Borders:
      • Lateral: Overlapped by the liver.
      • Medial: Related to:
        • Below: Celiac ganglion.
        • Above: Inferior phrenic artery.

Left Adrenal Gland

  • Shape: Semilunar
  • Parts:
    • Lower End: Rounded, anterior surface presents hilum.
    • Upper End: Narrow, related to the medial end of the spleen (Option B)
    • Anterior Surface:
      • Upper area: Related to the stomach bed.
      • Lower area: Overlapped by the body of the pancreas and crossed by the tortuous splenic artery.
    • Posterior Surface:
      • Lateral area: Related to the left kidney.
      • Medial area: Related to the left crus of the diaphragm.
    • Borders:
      • Lateral: Overlaps the left kidney.
      • Medial: Related to:
        • Below: Celiac ganglion.
        • Above: Inferior phrenic artery.

Yellow-colored structures (Option A): The adrenal cortex tends to exhibit a yellowish hue due to its higher fat content, while the adrenal medulla appears more reddish-brown in color.

It is located retroperitoneally (Option D): The adrenal glands are situated on top of each kidney in the retroperitoneal space.

questions.stem: Which of the following drains into the IVC?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following drains into the IVC?
questions.solution: 16927771979d068c6587">Renal Vein directly drains into the Inferior Vena Cava (IVC). This vein receives blood from the left kidney and left gonadal vein. Inferior vena cava: Origin: Formed by the union of the right and left common iliac veins at the level of L5 vertebra. Termination: Opens into the lower and posterior part of the right atrium. Course: It ascends along the front of the vertebral column, positioned to the right of the aorta, creates a groove on the posterior surface of the liver, and passes through the central tendon of the diaphragm at the T8 vertebral level. Tributaries of IVC Key features Right and left 3rd and 4th lumbar veins It drains the posterior, lateral, and anterior abdominal walls into IVC. Right gonadal vein Left gonadal vein drains into the left renal vein, which drains into the inferior vena cava. Right suprarenal vein Left suprarenal vein drains into the left renal vein, which drains into the inferior vena cava. Right inferior phrenic vein Left inferior phrenic vein drains into the left suprarenal, or left renal vein. Right and left renal veins Left renal vein (7.5cm) is three times longer than right renal vein (2.5cm) Hepatic veins Three large and many small veins open directly into the anterior surface of the inferior vena cava just before it pierces the diaphragm. Left Gonadal Vein (Option A): The left gonadal vein (left testicular vein in males or left ovarian vein in females) drains into the left renal vein, and then the blood flows into the IVC. Left adrenal vein (Option B): The left adrenal vein also drains into the left renal vein, which eventually connects to the IVC. Right ascending lumbar vein (Option D): Right ascending lumbar vein drain into the azygous vein Azygous vein is on right side Azygous will drain in Superior Vena Cava (SVC) at T4 level @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
16927771979d068c6587">Renal Vein directly drains into the Inferior Vena Cava (IVC). This vein receives blood from the left kidney and left gonadal vein.

 

 

Inferior vena cava:

  • Origin: Formed by the union of the right and left common iliac veins at the level of L5 vertebra.
  • Termination: Opens into the lower and posterior part of the right atrium.
  • Course: It ascends along the front of the vertebral column, positioned to the right of the aorta, creates a groove on the posterior surface of the liver, and passes through the central tendon of the diaphragm at the T8 vertebral level.

Tributaries of IVC

Key features

Right and left 3rd and 4th lumbar veins

It drains the posterior, lateral, and anterior abdominal walls into IVC.

Right gonadal vein

Left gonadal vein drains into the left renal vein, which drains into the inferior vena cava.

Right suprarenal vein

Left suprarenal vein drains into the left renal vein, which drains into the inferior vena cava.

Right inferior phrenic vein

Left inferior phrenic vein drains into the left suprarenal, or left renal vein.

Right and left renal veins

Left renal vein (7.5cm) is three times longer than right renal vein (2.5cm)

Hepatic veins

Three large and many small veins open directly into the anterior surface of the inferior vena cava just before it pierces the diaphragm.

Left Gonadal Vein (Option A):

The left gonadal vein (left testicular vein in males or left ovarian vein in females) drains into the left renal vein, and then the blood flows into the IVC.

Left adrenal vein (Option B):

The left adrenal vein also drains into the left renal vein, which eventually connects to the IVC.

Right ascending lumbar vein (Option D):

  • Right ascending lumbar vein drain into the azygous vein
  • Azygous vein is on right side
  • Azygous will drain in Superior Vena Cava (SVC) at T4 level

questions.stem: What is the name of the test performed in the image given below?
questions.stemHtml: What is the name of the test performed in the image given below?
questions.solution: the patency of radial and ulnar arteries supplying the hand. {{caption_text}} Allen's test: The examiner compresses both arteries at the wrist while the patient clenches their fist to drain blood from the hand. Subsequently, pressure on one artery is released, and the return of hand colour is observed. A rapid colour return indicates an adequate blood supply from that artery. It ensures an adequate collateral circulation and is especially useful before procedures such as arterial blood gas sampling or harvesting the radial artery for grafting. Incorrect Options: Adson test (Option B): Adson's test is a provocative test for Thoracic Outlet Syndrome accompanied by compression of the subclavian artery by a cervical rib or tightened anterior and middle scalene muscles. {{caption_text}} Barbeau test (Option C): The Barbeau test is another method for assessing the patency of the arterial palmar arch . It utilizes pulse oximetry and plethysmography to assess the palmar arches, so this choice is incorrect. Homan's test (Option D): The Homan's test is a physical examination procedure used to diagnose Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT) . A positive Homan’s sign in the presence of other clinical signs may be a quick indicator of DVT, so this choice is incorrect. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
the patency of radial and ulnar arteries supplying the hand.

 

Allen's test:

  • The examiner compresses both arteries at the wrist while the patient clenches their fist to drain blood from the hand.
  • Subsequently, pressure on one artery is released, and the return of hand colour is observed.
  • A rapid colour return indicates an adequate blood supply from that artery.
  • It ensures an adequate collateral circulation and is especially useful before procedures such as arterial blood gas sampling or harvesting the radial artery for grafting.

Incorrect Options:

Adson test (Option B): Adson's test is a provocative test for Thoracic Outlet Syndrome accompanied by compression of the subclavian artery by a cervical rib or tightened anterior and middle scalene muscles.

Barbeau test (Option C): The Barbeau test is another method for assessing the patency of the arterial palmar arch. It utilizes pulse oximetry and plethysmography to assess the palmar arches, so this choice is incorrect.

Homan's test (Option D): The Homan's test is a physical examination procedure used to diagnose Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT). A positive Homan’s sign in the presence of other clinical signs may be a quick indicator of DVT, so this choice is incorrect.

Osteochondroma:

Description
  • Also known as Exostosis
  • Most common primary benign bone tumor (but not a true bone tumor)
  • Benign cartilaginous neoplasms arising from physeal cartilage beneath the periosteum.
  • More common in males, usually appearing during adolescence.
  • Affects long bones, lower end of femur > upper end of tibia

Types
  • Solitary Osteochondroma
  • Multiple Osteochondromas (MO)

Clinical features
  • Painless mass- most common presentation
  • Pain: secondary to bursa formation/fracture/nerve compression

Radiographic Appearance
  • X-ray: Pedunculated cauliflower-like mass originating from metaphysis
  • MRI: used to assess cartilage thickness

Malignant transformation
  • Very rare
  • MRI showing cartilage thickness > 2 cms suggests malignant transformation (Option A)

Management
  • Asymptomatic cases: No treatment required
  • Symptomatic cases: Excision with biopsy

questions.solution: 79a">X-ray indicates grade-III injury of the Acromioclavicular joint as per Rockwood classification. In grade-III injury, both coracoclavicular and acromioclavicular ligaments are disrupted. {{caption_text}} Acromioclavicular joint injuries: Description Acute acromioclavicular (AC) joint injury, commonly following direct trauma; includes sprains, subluxations, and dislocations. Mechanism of Injury Fall on the shoulder with arm adducted leading to ligament strain or tear. Severe forces may cause complete dislocation. Classification Type I: AC ligament sprain; joint remains undisplaced. Type II: AC ligaments torn; joint subluxated with slight clavicle elevation. Type III: AC and coracoclavicular ligaments torn ; joint dislocated, visible step deformity. (Option C) Type IV: Posterior clavicle displacement. Type V: Marked upward clavicle displacement. Type VI: Inferior clavicle displacement beneath the coracoid. Clinical Features Signs: Pain, bruising, and tenderness at the injury site. Visible ‘step’ in cases of dislocation. Movement: Limited shoulder movement with severe pain in dislocation. X-ray Views: Anteroposterior, cephalic tilt, and axillary views are recommended. Stress view may differentiate Type II vs Type III. Stress View: Measure the distance between the coracoid and clavicle; >50% difference indicates dislocation. Treatment Sprains/Subluxations: Rest in a sling, pain subsides within a week, followed by shoulder exercises. Dislocations: Techniques include ligament reconstruction or clavicle excision. 79a">X-ray indicates grade-III injury of the Acromioclavicular joint as per Rockwood classification. In grade-III injury, both coracoclavicular and acromioclavicular ligaments are disrupted.

Acromioclavicular joint injuries:

Description
  • Acute acromioclavicular (AC) joint injury, commonly following direct trauma; includes sprains, subluxations, and dislocations.

Mechanism of Injury
  • Fall on the shoulder with arm adducted leading to ligament strain or tear. Severe forces may cause complete dislocation.

Classification
  • Type I: AC ligament sprain; joint remains undisplaced.
  • Type II: AC ligaments torn; joint subluxated with slight clavicle elevation.
  • Type III: AC and coracoclavicular ligaments torn; joint dislocated, visible step deformity. (Option C)
  • Type IV: Posterior clavicle displacement.
  • Type V: Marked upward clavicle displacement.
  • Type VI: Inferior clavicle displacement beneath the coracoid.

Clinical Features
  • Signs: Pain, bruising, and tenderness at the injury site. Visible ‘step’ in cases of dislocation.
  • Movement: Limited shoulder movement with severe pain in dislocation.

X-ray
  • Views: Anteroposterior, cephalic tilt, and axillary views are recommended. Stress view may differentiate Type II vs Type III.
  • Stress View: Measure the distance between the coracoid and clavicle; >50% difference indicates dislocation.

Treatment
  • Sprains/Subluxations: Rest in a sling, pain subsides within a week, followed by shoulder exercises.
  • Dislocations: Techniques include ligament reconstruction or clavicle excision.
  • Post-surgery Rehab: Elbow/forearm exercises day after surgery, shoulder movements 2 weeks later. Avoid strenuous lifting for 4–6 months.

Definition

The difference between the measured cations and the measured anions in the extracellular fluid (ECF).

Cations (Measured)

Sodium (Na⁺) and Potassium (K⁺)

Chloride (Cl⁻) and Bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻)

Protein anions, sulfate, phosphate, and organic acids.

Disadvantages: It may irritate nasal and pharyngeal mucosa. questions.stem: A neonate is brought to the pediatric ER in acute respiratory distress. On examination, the abdomen is scaphoid. Which of the following should not be performed in this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A neonate is brought to the pediatric ER in acute respiratory distress. On examination, the abdomen is scaphoid. Which of the following should not be performed in this patient?
questions.solution: A neonate with acute respiratory distress with a scaphoid could potentially be experiencing complications of a diaphragmatic hernia. Bag and Mask Ventilation is contraindicated in congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH) patients due to the risk of worsening respiratory distress and increasing intrathoracic pressure, which can further impede lung expansion and exacerbate the hernia. Management of Congenital Diaphragmatic Hernia: Initial Stabilization: Airway Management: Immediate endotracheal intubation (ET) is critical. (Option D ruled out) ECMO: If there is no response to ET Avoid excessive, mean airway pressure to prevent barotrauma Gastric Decompression: An orogastric tube is inserted to prevent gastric distention that worsens lung compression. Bag and Mask Ventilation is Contraindicated in CDH Surgical Repair is done only after pulmonary stabilisation in CDH (Immediate surgery done in case of Traumatic Hernia) PPV (Positive Pressure Ventilation) (Option A): This can be performed but should be done carefully to avoid overinflating the stomach, which can worsen respiratory distress. Intubation with PPV is preferred. Oxygen therapy (Option C): This is safe and can help improve oxygenation but is usually insufficient alone for severe respiratory distress in CDH. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: mMeta" data-dictid="baa24e9ba7169277719444ec43aa18">Orientia tsutsugamushi and transmitted by Trombiculid mites (chiggers). Characteristic eschar (necrotic ulcer with a black scab) is seen at the site of the mite bite. Common in farmers and individuals exposed to rural, wooded, or grassy areas. Other features include fever, thrombocytopenia, acute kidney injury (AKI), hepatosplenomegaly, and rash. Scrub typhus Causative agent Orientia tsutsugamushi - It differs from Rickettsia both genetically and by its cell wall composition i.e. it lacks lipopolysaccharide layer . Vector Chiggers (larvae of trombiculid mite) Pathophysiology Scrub typhus is so named because it occurs in areas of scrub vegetation i.e. low lying trees and bushes. It is transmitted by the bite of infected trombiculid mites. Among all stages of mite, the larvae (called chiggers) are the only stage that feed on humans . Hence, scrub typhus is also called chiggerosis . Mites can maintain the organisms through transovarial transmission . Orientia tsutsugamushi infects mononuclear cells but still produces fever and rash. Clinical features The classic presentation of scrub typhus consists of triad of an eschar (at the site of bite), regional lymphadenopathy and maculopapular rash sparing palms and soles. Non-specific manifestations may appear early such as fever, headache, myalgia, cough, and gastrointestinal symptoms. Complications such as encephalitis and interstitial pneumonia may occur rarely in the late stage (due to vascular injury). Investigations The Weil-Felix test shows OX K+ only. Treatment Doxycycline is the drug choice. Azithromycin is given alternatively and the drug of choice in children and pregnant women . Anthrax (Option B): Cutaneous anthrax presents with painless ulcers with black eschar but has extensive surrounding edema and is more commonly seen in individuals handling animal hides or wool. Leptospirosis (Option C): Causes Weil’s disease with jaundice, renal failure, and hemorrhage, but does not present with an eschar. Common in farmers exposed to rodent-contaminated water. Brucellosis (Option D): Presents with undulant fever, arthralgia, hepatosplenomegaly, and endocarditis, but no eschar is seen. More common in people working with livestock or unpasteurized dairy products. @Neet_pg_bot

Causative agent

Leptospirosis (Option C): Causes Weil’s disease with jaundice, renal failure, and hemorrhage, but does not present with an eschar. Common in farmers exposed to rodent-contaminated water.

questions.stemHtml: What should be the next course of action in managing a patient with pneumonia who is on a ventilator, weighs 50 kg, has a respiratory rate of 14 breaths per minute, a bicarbonate level of 18, a pH of 7.33, a paCO2 level of 48 mmHg, a Pao2 level of 110 mmHg, a PEEP of 12 cm H₂O, a tidal volume of 420 mL, and a SpO2 level of 100% with an FiO2 of 90%?
questions.solution: ve Ventilation is the current standard in mechanical ventilation. If Fio2 > 60%, oxygen radical formation can occur causing worsening of symptoms. FIO2 has to be decreased in this patient to prevent free radical formation and since PaO2 is higher than normal. Clinical Modes of Management in ARDS Lung Protective Ventilation (LPV): Tidal volumes : ≤6 mL/kg of ideal body weight to prevent alveolar overdistension. (Option D ruled out) PEEP : Use moderate levels to avoid alveolar collapse. (Option A ruled out) Plateau pressure : Limit to ≤30 cm H₂O to minimize barotrauma and pneumothorax. Permissive hypercapnia : Allow mild-to-moderate respiratory acidosis to avoid lung injury. (Option C ruled out) FiO₂ : Minimize while targeting PaO₂ >55 mmHg or SpO₂ >88%. (Option B) Recruitment Strategies: Use of PEEP to recruit collapsed alveoli and improve oxygenation. Prone positioning : Shown to improve survival in severe ARDS (P/F ratio ≤150). Advanced Techniques: Neuromuscular blockade : Early use may benefit patients with severe ARDS (P/F ratio <150). ECMO : Considered for severe, refractory ARDS in specialized centers. Rescue Therapies (Limited evidence for survival benefit): High-frequency oscillatory ventilation : No significant outcome improvements. Inhaled vasodilators (iNO, prostaglandins): Transient oxygenation improvement but no long-term benefit. Fluid Management: Conservative fluid management : Improves oxygenation and ventilator-free days. Corticosteroids : Mixed results; may benefit ARDS from bacterial sepsis but not viral pneumonia (except SARS-CoV2). @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Which part of the haemoglobin molecule does 2,3-Bisphosphoglycerate (2,3-BPG) bind to in order to regulate oxygen release?
questions.stemHtml: Which part of the haemoglobin molecule does 2,3-Bisphosphoglycerate (2,3-BPG) bind to in order to regulate oxygen release?
questions.solution: ong>Explanation: 2,3-BPG binds within the central cavity of the deoxyhaemoglobin tetramer . It interacts with positively charged residues (mainly lysine and histidine ) on the β-chains . This binding stabilises the T (tense) state , lowering haemoglobin’s affinity for oxygen and promoting oxygen delivery to tissues. Effect of 2,3 BPG on Hb: Reduces the affinity of Hb for oxygen and helps unload oxygen to tissues. A by-product of glycolysis. (Rapaport Leubering Cycle) Alpha chains of haemoglobin (Option A) : Incorrect because 2,3-BPG binds primarily to residues on the β-chains , not the α-chains. Heme iron centre (Option B) : 2,3-BPG does not bind directly to heme or iron ; it acts allosterically , not at the active oxygen-binding site. Globin-heme interface (Option D) : This is the site of coordination between globin and heme, not where 2,3-BPG binds. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solutionHtml:
11fdf3e9911">ALT >1000

Explanation:

  • Severe dengue (Dengue hemorrhagic fever grade III & IV / Dengue shock syndrome) criteria include:
    • Severe plasma leakage → leading to shock or fluid accumulation (pleural effusion/ascites).
    • Severe bleeding.
    • Severe organ involvement:
      • Liver: AST/ALT >1000 U/L (marker of severe hepatitis).
      • CNS involvement: Encephalitis, seizures.
      • Myocarditis, renal failure.

Clinical presentation of Dengue:

Uncategorised fever

  • No typical features

Break bone fever

(Classical dengue fever/ acute viral infection)

 
  • Retro orbital pain
  • Arthralgia
  • Severe myalgia and headache
  • Bimodal presentation of fever:
    • 39-40°C, peaks on days 1-2
    • Resurges: day 5-6
    • Recovery: day 7-10.
  • Rash: pin-point eruptions on the face, neck and chest followed by maculopapular or scarlatiniform on 3rd or 4th day.

Dengue haemorrhagic syndrome
  • Dengue fever + hemorrhagic manifestations(bleeding from any orifice)
  • Rash: Maculopapular/ Rubelliform
  • Lab diagnosis
    • 20% increase in hematocrit
    • Thrombocytopenia (<1 lac)
  • Clinical diagnosis
    • Tourniquet test- >10 petechiae/ sq inch area

Dengue shock syndrome
  • Pulse pressure - <20 mmHg
  • Mean systolic pressure - <90mmHg: adults, <80 mmHg: children.

Dengue complications

Neurological
  • Dengue encephalopathy is most commonly encountered neurological complication of dengue virus
    • linked primarily to dengue hemorrhagic fever and dengue shock syndrome
    • EEG may show abnormalities such as burst suppression and seizures
    • CSF profiles typically remain normal.
    • Neuroimaging can be normal or reveal diffuse cerebral edema.
  • Encephalitis
  • GBS
  • Stroke

Cardiomyopathy
  • Dengue virus-induced dilated cardiomyopathy should always be considered if a dengue fever patient has refractory shock and signs and symptoms of congestive heart failure.

Hepatic injury
  • Liver involvement in dengue is a crucial feature
  • The effect ranges from an asymptomatic rise in liver enzymes to the development of ALF
  • The most common atypical manifestation reported was hepatitis

Pneumonia

 
  • Staphylococcus pneumonia is an important accompanying problem seen in dengue patient
  • co-infection between dengue and influenza can result in exacerbation of pneumonia

Orchitis

 
  • Orchitis usually occurs together with epididymitis
  • Commonly seen in men between 14 and 35 years of age.

Dengue Hemorrhagic Fever

All of the following:

  • Acute onset of fever
  • 2-7 days duration
  • Hemorrhagic manifestations
    • Positive tourniquet test/Petechiae
    • Ecchymosis
    • Purpura/Bleeding from mucosa, GIT, Injection sites, etc
  • Platelet count ≤ 100,000 cells/cu.mm.
  • Plasma leakage
    • Rising hematocrit
      • Hemoconcentration >20%
    • Pleural effusion, ascites/Hypoproteinemia)

Dengue Shock Syndrome
  • DHF criteria plus Signs of Shock
  • Tachycardia/Cool extremities/Weak pulse/Lethargy/Restlessness
  • Pulse pressure <20 mm Hg with increased Diastolic pressure (e.g. 100/80)
  • Hypotension (Systolic <80 mm Hg for age <5 years/80-90 mm Hg for older children and adults)

Leucopenia plus thrombocytopenia (Option A): Thrombocytopenia (<100,000/mm³) and leucopenia are common findings in dengue fever, but they do not indicate severe dengue unless associated with bleeding, shock, or organ involvement.

Persistent vomiting (Option B): It is a warning sign for dengue progression, but alone does not classify as severe dengue.

Hepatomegaly >1 cm (Option C): Mild hepatomegaly is seen in dengue, but it becomes severe only when associated with AST/ALT >1000 U/L.

questions.stem: An 18-day-old baby presents with fever and cough. On examination, vesicles are observed over the trunk and upper limb. The mother had genital ulcers one year ago, which have since resolved. Biopsy of the vesicles reveals multinucleated giant cells. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: An 18-day-old baby presents with fever and cough. On examination, vesicles are observed over the trunk and upper limb. The mother had genital ulcers one year ago, which have since resolved. Biopsy of the vesicles reveals multinucleated giant cells. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: class="customMeta" data-dictid="17df0c44e116927771897deca1bbf4">HSV infection typically results from vertical transmission during vaginal delivery, especially if the mother had genital HSV infection. The presence of vesicles in a newborn with a maternal history of genital ulcers strongly suggests neonatal herpes simplex infection. Microscopic features Tzanck smear: Multinucleated giant cells with faceted nuclei and homogeneously stained 'ground-glass' chromatin ( Tzanck cells ). Formation of Lipschutz bodies (Cowdry type A). {{caption_text}} Molluscum contagiosum virus (MCV) (Option B): MCV causes pearly, dome-shaped papules with central umbilication, not vesicles. Human papillomavirus (HPV) (Option C): HPV is associated with warts, not vesicular lesions. Varicella (Option D) : Varicella (chickenpox) also causes vesicular rash, but it is less likely in a neonate unless there is maternal varicella exposure close to delivery. Multinucleated giant cells can be seen in both HSV and VZV, but maternal history of genital ulcers favors HSV over varicella. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solutionHtml:
Correct Option: A) Orbital cellulitis

  • The given CT is confirmatory of orbital cellulitis as there is proptosis visible on the CT and the patient is also having orbital pain.

Orbital Cellulitis

Definition
  • Orbital cellulitis is an acute infection of the soft tissues of the orbit located behind the orbital septum.

Etiology
  • Exogenous Infection: Occurs due to penetrating injuries. Example: foreign body retention, surgical procedures like evisceration, enucleation, orbitotomy, dacryocystectomy.
  • Endogenous Infection: From metastatic infections. Example: breast abscess, puerperal sepsis, thrombophlebitis, septicemia
  • Extension from Neighboring Structures (most common): Paranasal sinuses (most common: ethmoid sinus), teeth, face, eyelids, intracranial cavity, and intraorbital structures.

Clinical Features

Symptoms:

  • Swelling and severe pain (worsened by eye movement or pressure).
  • Systemic symptoms: fever, nausea, vomiting, prostration.
  • Vision loss and/or diplopia in moderate to advanced cases.

Signs:

  • Swelling of lids with woody hardness and redness.
  • Chemosis (conjunctival swelling), which may lead to necrosis.
  • Axial proptosis.
  • Restricted eye movements.
  • RAPD (Relative Afferent Pupillary Defect) may occur due to optic neuropathy or central retinal artery occlusion.
  • Fundus examination may show retinal vein congestion, papillitis, or papilledema

Staging

Modified Chandler staging system:

  • Stage I: Preseptal cellulitis/ periorbital cellulitis (limited anterior to orbital septum)
  • Stage II: Inflammatory orbital oedema/ Orbital cellulitis (Posterior to orbital septum)
  • Stage III: Subperiosteal abscess
  • Stage IV: Orbital abscess
  • Stage V: Cavernous sinus thrombosis

Investigations
  • Cultures: Nasal, conjunctival, and blood samples for bacterial culture.
  • Complete Blood Count: Leukocytosis.
  • X-ray PNS: To detect sinusitis.
    • Orbital Ultrasonography: To detect orbital abscesses.
  • CT Scan/MRI: Differentiates preseptal from postseptal cellulitis, detects abscesses, intracranial extension, and guides surgical drainage.

Incorrect Options:

Sinusitis (Option B): This option is incorrect as proptosis is visible on imaging.

Both A and B (Option C): This option is also incorrect.

Periosteal abscess (Option D): This option is incorrect as CT findings of periosteal abscess show abscess behind the orbit.

questions.stem: Which of the following is/are advantages of a saline mount compared to an iodine mount in stool microscopy? 1. Motility of trophozoites 2. Internal structure of cysts 3. Differentiate bile stained and non bile stained
questions.stemHtml:
Which of the following is/are advantages of a saline mount compared to an iodine mount in stool microscopy?
1. Motility of trophozoites
2. Internal structure of cysts
3. Differentiate bile stained and non bile stained
questions.solution: tid="894da1dfe6169277719871d7210619">Saline Wet Mount) - Advantages: Motility of trophozoites (Statement 1) → Saline mount preserves the natural motility of protozoan trophozoites (e.g., Giardia lamblia shows "falling leaf" motility, Entamoeba histolytica shows directional motility). Differentiation of bile-stained vs non-bile-stained ova (Statement 3) → Saline mount allows observation of color differences, making it useful to distinguish bile-stained ova (e.g., Ascaris lumbricoides fertilized eggs) from non-bile-stained ones. Internal Structure of Cysts( Statement 3) → Iodine mount is better for cyst structures. Iodine stains the glycogen and nuclei of protozoan cysts, improving visualization of internal structures (e.g., Entamoeba histolytica, Giardia lamblia cysts). Saline mount does not enhance internal details well. Stool sample processing Microscopic examination of stool samples This is done by two methods: Direct wet mount examination Permanent staining methods Direct wet mount Preparation: Drops of saline and Lugol’s iodine are used on the left and right sides of the slide. Mix ~2 mg of feces to form a smooth suspension. Place a coverslip on the mount for examination under a microscope. Observation: Trophozoites Normal constituents of stool like plant fibers and starch cells can be seen Cellular Elements: Pus cells (in inflammatory diarrhea) Red blood cells (in dysentery) Charcot-Leyden Crystals {{caption_text}} {{caption_text}} Types of wet mounts: Saline mount: Uses: Detects trophozoites, cysts, helminth eggs, and larvae. Advantages: Demonstrates motility of trophozoites and larvae. Bile staining property can be assessed (bile-stained eggs appear golden brown). Iodine mount: Advantages: Better visualization of nuclear details in cysts, larvae, and eggs. Disadvantages: Iodine immobilizes and kills parasites , hindering motility observation. Bile staining property cannot be assessed. Permanent stained smears {{caption_text}} This method stains the internal structures. Purpose: For accurate detection of protozoan cysts and trophozoites. Common Stains: Iron-hematoxylin stain. Trichrome stain. Modified acid-fast stain for coccidian parasites (e.g., Cryptosporidium). Sedimentation techniques and Flotation techniques are concentration techniques used to recover low numbers of parasites in stool samples. Useful for epidemiological studies and assessing treatment response. Detects eggs, cysts, and larvae but does not detect trophozoites, as these get destroyed in the process . Sedimentation techniques : Eggs and cysts settle at the bottom due to higher density. Example: Formalin-ether concentration increases detection sensitivity by 8–10 times. Flotation techniques : Specimens are suspended in a denser medium (e.g., saturated salt solution) in which the eggs and cysts float. Limitations: Cannot concentrate non-floating parasites (e.g., unfertilized Ascaris eggs). @Neet_pg_bot

tid="894da1dfe6169277719871d7210619">Saline Wet Mount) - Advantages:
  • Motility of trophozoites (Statement 1) → Saline mount preserves the natural motility of protozoan trophozoites (e.g., Giardia lamblia shows "falling leaf" motility, Entamoeba histolytica shows directional motility).
  • Differentiation of bile-stained vs non-bile-stained ova (Statement 3) → Saline mount allows observation of color differences, making it useful to distinguish bile-stained ova (e.g., Ascaris lumbricoides fertilized eggs) from non-bile-stained ones.

Internal Structure of Cysts( Statement 3) → Iodine mount is better for cyst structures.

  • Iodine stains the glycogen and nuclei of protozoan cysts, improving visualization of internal structures (e.g., Entamoeba histolytica, Giardia lamblia cysts). Saline mount does not enhance internal details well.

Stool sample processing

Microscopic examination of stool samples

This is done by two methods:

  • Direct wet mount examination
  • Permanent staining methods

Direct wet mount

Preparation:

  • Drops of saline and Lugol’s iodine are used on the left and right sides of the slide.
  • Mix ~2 mg of feces to form a smooth suspension.
  • Place a coverslip on the mount for examination under a microscope.

Observation:

  • Trophozoites
  • Normal constituents of stool like plant fibers and starch cells can be seen
  • Cellular Elements:
    • Pus cells (in inflammatory diarrhea)
    • Red blood cells (in dysentery)
  • Charcot-Leyden Crystals

 

 

Types of wet mounts:

Saline mount:

  • Uses: Detects trophozoites, cysts, helminth eggs, and larvae.
  • Advantages:
    • Demonstrates motility of trophozoites and larvae.
    • Bile staining property can be assessed (bile-stained eggs appear golden brown).

Iodine mount:

  • Advantages: Better visualization of nuclear details in cysts, larvae, and eggs.
  • Disadvantages:
    • Iodine immobilizes and kills parasites, hindering motility observation.
    • Bile staining property cannot be assessed.

Permanent stained smears

 
  • This method stains the internal structures.
  • Purpose: For accurate detection of protozoan cysts and trophozoites.
  • Common Stains:
    • Iron-hematoxylin stain.
    • Trichrome stain.
    • Modified acid-fast stain for coccidian parasites (e.g., Cryptosporidium).

 

Sedimentation techniques and Flotation techniques are concentration techniques used to recover low numbers of parasites in stool samples.

  • Useful for epidemiological studies and assessing treatment response.
  • Detects eggs, cysts, and larvae but does not detect trophozoites, as these get destroyed in the process.
  • Sedimentation techniques:
      • Eggs and cysts settle at the bottom due to higher density.
      • Example: Formalin-ether concentration increases detection sensitivity by 8–10 times.
    • Flotation techniques:
      • Specimens are suspended in a denser medium (e.g., saturated salt solution) in which the eggs and cysts float.
      • Limitations: Cannot concentrate non-floating parasites (e.g., unfertilized Ascaris eggs).

questions.stem: Which bacterial toxin acts by interfering with the function of elongation factor-2 (EF-2)?
questions.stemHtml: Which bacterial toxin acts by interfering with the function of elongation factor-2 (EF-2)?
questions.solution: htheria toxin (Produced by Corynebacterium diphtheriae), ADP-ribosylates elongation factor-2 (EF-2), leading to inhibition of protein synthesis. This results in cell death, leading to pseudomembrane formation in the pharynx and systemic complications like myocarditis and neuropathy. Diphtheria Toxin Production and Structure DT is a protein exotoxin produced by the toxigenic Corynebacterium diphtheriae. Consists of two fragments (Bipartite), A and B, with a molecular weight of approximately 62,000 daltons. Role of Lysogenic β-phage The tox gene is carried by a lysogenic β-phage. Only phage-infected strains produce toxin; nontoxigenic strains can become toxigenic if infected. Corynebacterium diphtheriae remains localized at the infection site, with only the toxin entering circulation, causing toxaemia but not bacteremia. Mechanism of Action Fragment B binds host cell receptors, facilitating fragment A entry into the cytoplasm. Fragment A catalyses ADP-ribosylation of EF-2, halting protein synthesis. Systemic Effects DT spreads via blood, causing myocarditis and neuritis. Myocarditis is potentially fatal. Factors Affecting Production Influenced by environmental factors: alkaline pH (7.8-8.0), oxygen, and iron concentration in the growth medium. High production with low iron availability; iron addition inhibits production. Toxoid Formation Treatment with formalin (0.2-0.4%), and incubation at 37°C for 4-6 weeks converts DT to toxoid. Toxoid lacks toxicity but induces an immune response; used in vaccines. Immunity Immunity is primarily mediated by antitoxin antibodies neutralizing DT. Clostridium toxin (Option B) : Clostridium species produce neurotoxins that act by blocking neurotransmitter release, not EF-2 inhibition. Bacillus toxin (Option C) : Bacillus anthracis produces anthrax toxin (PA, EF, LF), which disrupts cell signaling via adenylate cyclase, not EF-2 inhibition. Vibrio toxin (Option D): Vibrio cholerae produces cholera toxin, which increases cAMP via ADP-ribosylation of Gs protein, causing watery diarrhea but does not affect EF-2. @Neet_pg_bot

htheria toxin (Produced by Corynebacterium diphtheriae), ADP-ribosylates elongation factor-2 (EF-2), leading to inhibition of protein synthesis.
  • This results in cell death, leading to pseudomembrane formation in the pharynx and systemic complications like myocarditis and neuropathy.

 

Diphtheria Toxin

Production and Structure
  • DT is a protein exotoxin produced by the toxigenic Corynebacterium diphtheriae.
  • Consists of two fragments (Bipartite), A and B, with a molecular weight of approximately 62,000 daltons.

Role of Lysogenic β-phage
  • The tox gene is carried by a lysogenic β-phage.
  • Only phage-infected strains produce toxin; nontoxigenic strains can become toxigenic if infected.
  • Corynebacterium diphtheriae remains localized at the infection site, with only the toxin entering circulation, causing toxaemia but not bacteremia.

Mechanism of Action
  • Fragment B binds host cell receptors, facilitating fragment A entry into the cytoplasm.
  • Fragment A catalyses ADP-ribosylation of EF-2, halting protein synthesis.

Systemic Effects
  • DT spreads via blood, causing myocarditis and neuritis.
  • Myocarditis is potentially fatal.

Factors Affecting Production
  • Influenced by environmental factors: alkaline pH (7.8-8.0), oxygen, and iron concentration in the growth medium.
  • High production with low iron availability; iron addition inhibits production.

Toxoid Formation
  • Treatment with formalin (0.2-0.4%), and incubation at 37°C for 4-6 weeks converts DT to toxoid.
  • Toxoid lacks toxicity but induces an immune response; used in vaccines.

Immunity
  • Immunity is primarily mediated by antitoxin antibodies neutralizing DT.

 

Clostridium toxin (Option B): Clostridium species produce neurotoxins that act by blocking neurotransmitter release, not EF-2 inhibition.

Bacillus toxin (Option C): Bacillus anthracis produces anthrax toxin (PA, EF, LF), which disrupts cell signaling via adenylate cyclase, not EF-2 inhibition.

Vibrio toxin (Option D): Vibrio cholerae produces cholera toxin, which increases cAMP via ADP-ribosylation of Gs protein, causing watery diarrhea but does not affect EF-2.

Tests for Diagnosing Stapedial Otosclerosis

  • Otoscopy
    • Examines external and middle ear.
    • Identifies abnormalities; typically, the tympanic membrane appears normal in otosclerosis.
  • Fistula Test
    • Evaluates inner ear response to pressure changes.
    • Helps diagnose conditions like superior semicircular canal dehiscence, especially with vertigo.
  • Tuning Fork Tests
    • Weber and Rinne's tests differentiate conductive from sensorineural hearing loss.
    • Less sensitive than audiometry but useful when other findings are inconclusive.
  • Audiometry
    • Pure-tone Audiometry
      • Diagnoses and characterizes hearing loss.
      • Initial low-frequency conductive loss progresses to flat maximal loss as stapes become fixed.
      • Carhart effect may reduce bone conduction thresholds, noticeable at 2 kHz.

    • Speech Audiometry
      • Assesses speech understanding
      • High speech recognition with appropriate hearing aids.
    • Stapedial Reflex Testing
      • Assesses stapedius muscle response to sound.
      • Reflex is often absent or abnormal in otosclerosis.
    • Tympanometry
      • Measures tympanic membrane and middle ear system mobility.
      • Mobility is usually normal, but compliance may be low.
      • Helps exclude other middle ear conditions.
  • Imaging
    • High-Resolution CT Scan
      • Sensitive and specific for active otosclerosis.
      • Reveals hypodense lesions in active disease.
      • Less effective for inactive disease due to dense otic capsule.

Rinne’s Test - positive; Weber’s Test - lateralized to right ear (Option B): In otosclerosis there is a conductive type of hearing loss hence Rinne will be negative.

HIV is a spherical virus and its capsid has an icosahedral symmetry and also contains two copies of single-stranded positive-sense RNA in its core.

Structure of HIV

  • HIV is a spherical virus measuring 80–110 nm in diameter and belongs to the lentivirus family. Its structure includes:
  • Envelope: Composed of:
    • Lipid Component: Derived from the host cell membrane.

questions.stem: A patient on anti-PD1 immunotherapy (nivolumab) comes with pruritis, eczema, and urticarial rashes. Histopathological examination reveals a subepidermal blister and direct immunofluorescence of the lesions showed linear C3 and IgG on basement membrane. What isthe diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A patient on anti-PD1 immunotherapy (nivolumab) comes with pruritis, eczema, and urticarial rashes. Histopathological examination reveals a subepidermal blister and direct immunofluorescence of the lesions showed linear C3 and IgG on basement membrane. What isthe diagnosis?
questions.solution: BP is a common subepidermal immunobullous disorder mainly affecting elder people. Autoantibodies against hemidesmosomal target proteins BP230(BPAG1) and BP180(BPAG2) which finally leads to bullae formation. It is characterised by a prodromal non bullous stage with pruritis which is followed by a bullous stage. The later has intense pruritus with tense blisters and vesicles. These blisters show a negative Nikolsky sign but a positive Bulla spread sign. The rupture of blisters leads to yellow or hemorrhagic crust formation, which later heal without any scar. Oral lesions can occur sometimes. HPE shows a subepidermal split with inflammatory infiltrate, immunofluorescence shows a linear binding of immunoglobulin (IgG and C3) at the dermo-epidermal junction. Topical and systemic steroids are the mainstay of treatment. {{caption_text}} Dermatitis herpetiformis (Option A) DH is a gluten-sensitive enteropathy associated with deposition of IgA in the dermal papillae, not linear IgG or C3 at the basement membrane. DH typically shows granular IgA deposition in immunofluorescence and not the linear patterns seen here. Pemphigus vulgaris (Option B) PV is characterized by intraepidermal blistering and acantholysis (loss of cell-to-cell adhesion between keratinocytes). Immunofluorescence shows intercellular IgG (not linear staining at the basement membrane zone). The presence of subepidermal blisters here excludes PV. Pemphigus foliaceous (Option C) PF is another type of pemphigus that features intraepidermal blistering and acantholysis but lacks subepidermal blistering. Immunofluorescence in PF typically shows intercellular IgG, not the linear IgG and C3 at the basement membrane observed in this case. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: eta" data-dictid="40ebcbf95e169277718613d7c2d999">ECG findings (ST elevation in V1-V3), the diagnosis is Brugada Syndrome - a rare, inherited cardiac disorder that predisposes individuals to life-threatening arrhythmias, often occurring during sleep. The presence of agonal respiration at night strongly suggests a ventricular arrhythmia, a hallmark of Brugada Syndrome. Brugada Syndrome

About

A rare, inherited disease that predisposes patients to potentially fatal cardiac arrhythmias, characterised by right bundle branch block and ST-segment elevations in the right precordial leads (V1-V3) on ECG.

Clinical features
  • Symptoms range from asymptomatic to sudden cardiac death, often during sleep.

  • Other symptoms: Palpitations, dizziness, and fever history may trigger symptoms.

Drug challenge test

Empiric Therapy: Outpatient: No comorbidities: Monotherapy with macrolides (Azithromycin, Clarithromycin). With comorbidities (chronic lung/heart disease, diabetes, smoking, HIV): Newer fluoroquinolones (Levofloxacin, Moxifloxacin, Gemifloxacin) or a combination of beta-lactam (e.g., amoxicillin) and a macrolide. Inpatient Non-ICU: Newer fluoroquinolones (Levofloxacin, Moxifloxacin) alone or a combination of beta-lactam (e.g., Ampicillin, Ceftriaxone) and a macrolide. Influenza Treatment: All hospitalized patients testing positive for influenza should receive Oseltamivir, regardless of illness onset. questions.solution: The patient might be suffering from a scorpion sting cardiotoxicity as per his symptoms and the best choice of medication here is Prazosin . Treatment of scorpion sting: Identification of the scorpion species is essential for determining treatment, as stings from non-lethal species typically only require basic care. Non-lethal stings : Most stings cause local discomfort and can be managed at home with ice packs, analgesics, or antihistamines. Patients should return to the emergency department if cranial-nerve or neuromuscular symptoms develop. Severe envenomations : Aggressive supportive care and careful use of antivenom can prevent deaths from more dangerous stings. Initial measures : Keeping the patient calm, applying pressure dressings, and using cold packs can reduce venom absorption. Treatment for symptoms : Continuous IV infusion of midazolam can control agitation and muscle movements, but close monitoring is needed due to the risk of respiratory arrest, especially when sedatives or narcotics are used. Management of complications : Hypertension and Pulmonary oedema : Managed with Nifedipine, Nitroprusside, Hydralazine, or Prazosin . Bradycardia : Managed with atropine. Antivenin : FDA-approved antivenin (C. sculpturatus IgG F(ab')2 in horse serum) is available in some countries and can rapidly reverse cranial-nerve dysfunction and muscular symptoms when administered intravenously. Incorrect Options: Anti-snake venom (Option A) is a specific treatment used for snakebite envenomation and is not indicated in the given scenario. Adrenaline (Option B) is commonly used in emergencies to treat severe allergic reactions and cardiac arrest. questions.stem: A 45-year-old male comes with recurrent blisters and oral ulcers for 3 years. The histology is as shown. What is the diagnosis of this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A 45-year-old male comes with recurrent blisters and oral ulcers for 3 years. The histology is as shown. What is the diagnosis of this patient?
questions.solution: Explanation: The above clinical features and HPE findings in this patient suggest the diagnosis of Pemphigus vulgaris (PV), which most commonly has antibodies against Desmoglein 3. Pemphigus vulgaris: PV is the most common chronic autoimmune blistering disease caused by antibodies against desmosomal adhesion proteins. They are characterized by the presence of flaccid blisters filled with clear fluid present on normal skin or an erythematous base. The blisters rupture producing painful erosion. Mucosal involvement is a very important and one of the distinguishing features of PV. Histopathology: Intraepidermal cleavage with acantholysis (detached keratinocytes) primarily localized to the suprabasal region Separation of basal keratinocytes along the basement membrane zone, resulting in an appearance that resembles a "row of tombstones" The target antigens for PV are most commonly Desmoglein 3 and sometimes Desmoglein 1. The image below shows the common target antigen in Intraepidermal Immunobullous Disorders. Dermatitis herpetiformis (Option B) Associated with celiac disease and characterized by intensely pruritic, grouped vesicles typically on extensor surfaces. Shows granular IgA deposits on immunofluorescence, not intercellular IgG. Bullous pemphigoid (Option C) Causes subepidermal blisters and does not commonly present with oral ulcers. Immunofluorescence shows linear IgG and C3 at the dermal-epidermal junction. Linear IgA disease (Option D) Characterized by linear IgA deposits at the basement membrane zone. Typically causes subepidermal blistering, not intraepidermal, and oral ulcers are less common. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
Explanation:

The above clinical features and HPE findings in this patient suggest the diagnosis of Pemphigus vulgaris (PV), which most commonly has antibodies against Desmoglein 3.

Pemphigus vulgaris:

  • PV is the most common chronic autoimmune blistering disease caused by antibodies against desmosomal adhesion proteins.
  • They are characterized by the presence of flaccid blisters filled with clear fluid present on normal skin or an erythematous base.
  • The blisters rupture producing painful erosion.
  • Mucosal involvement is a very important and one of the distinguishing features of PV.
  • Histopathology:
    • Intraepidermal cleavage with acantholysis (detached keratinocytes) primarily localized to the suprabasal region
    • Separation of basal keratinocytes along the basement membrane zone, resulting in an appearance that resembles a "row of tombstones"

The target antigens for PV are most commonly Desmoglein 3 and sometimes Desmoglein 1. The image below shows the common target antigen in Intraepidermal Immunobullous Disorders.

Dermatitis herpetiformis (Option B)

  • Associated with celiac disease and characterized by intensely pruritic, grouped vesicles typically on extensor surfaces.
  • Shows granular IgA deposits on immunofluorescence, not intercellular IgG.

Bullous pemphigoid (Option C)

  • Causes subepidermal blisters and does not commonly present with oral ulcers.
  • Immunofluorescence shows linear IgG and C3 at the dermal-epidermal junction.

Linear IgA disease (Option D)

  • Characterized by linear IgA deposits at the basement membrane zone.
  • Typically causes subepidermal blistering, not intraepidermal, and oral ulcers are less common.

questions.solution: dictid="59ff8b38191692777201150e72ebc3">uterine inversion with the placenta still attached, the immediate priority is to reposition the uterus without removing the placenta to prevent further hemorrhage and uterine contraction, which would complicate repositioning. The management of uterine inversion should follow the following steps: Immediate call for assistance (obstetric and anaesthesia personnel) Blood is brought to the delivery room to use when needed Two large bore IV lines are secured, and crystalloids are given to treat hypovolemia till the blood is brought The woman is evaluated for emergency general anaesthesia Stop tocolytics Start oxytocin Give antibiotics The steps of management of uterine inversion according to certain factors are as follows: Condition Method Inverted uterus not contracted and retracted completely The placenta has already separated Replace the uterus by pushing the inverted fundus using your palm and fingers The placenta is still attached Reposition the uterus with the placenta in situ Tocolytics may be used for uterine relaxation If they fail, general anaesthesia (inhalational) is used The uterus is replaced, and the placenta removed Failed uterine reposition with attached placenta The placenta is peeled off, and repositioning is attempted again Failed manual repositioning Surgical repositioning (Huntington’s procedure) Manually removing the placenta and repositioning the uterus (Option A) will lead to increased haemorrhage and faster contraction of the uterus, making it difficult to replace the uterus. Hence, this is not the preferred step. Shift to the operating theatre (OT) and reinsert the uterus under general anaesthesia (Option C): General anesthesia and surgical repositioning are reserved for failed manual repositioning attempts. Start oxytocin infusion (Option D) : If oxytocin infusion is continued, the uterus will contract and lead to difficulty in its repositioning, so tocolytics are used to relax the uterus, and then once the repositioning is completed, oxytocin infusion and bimanual compression are started to aid uterine contraction. @Neet_pg_bot

The management of uterine inversion should follow the following steps:

  • Immediate call for assistance (obstetric and anaesthesia personnel)
  • Blood is brought to the delivery room to use when needed
  • Two large bore IV lines are secured, and crystalloids are given to treat hypovolemia till the blood is brought
  • The woman is evaluated for emergency general anaesthesia
  • Stop tocolytics
  • Start oxytocin
  • Give antibiotics

 

The steps of management of uterine inversion according to certain factors are as follows:

Condition

Method

  • Inverted uterus not contracted and retracted completely
  • The placenta has already separated

Replace the uterus by pushing the inverted fundus using your palm and fingers

The placenta is still attached
  • Reposition the uterus with the placenta in situ
  • Tocolytics may be used for uterine relaxation
  • If they fail, general anaesthesia (inhalational) is used
  • The uterus is replaced, and the placenta removed

Failed uterine reposition with attached placenta

The placenta is peeled off, and repositioning is attempted again

Failed manual repositioning

Surgical repositioning (Huntington’s procedure)

 

 

Manually removing the placenta and repositioning the uterus (Option A) will lead to increased haemorrhage and faster contraction of the uterus, making it difficult to replace the uterus. Hence, this is not the preferred step.

Shift to the operating theatre (OT) and reinsert the uterus under general anaesthesia (Option C): General anesthesia and surgical repositioning are reserved for failed manual repositioning attempts.

Start oxytocin infusion (Option D): If oxytocin infusion is continued, the uterus will contract and lead to difficulty in its repositioning, so tocolytics are used to relax the uterus, and then once the repositioning is completed, oxytocin infusion and bimanual compression are started to aid uterine contraction.

Management of placenta accreta spectrum

Placenta Accreta Type

Management

Partial Placenta Accreta

 
  • Remove as much placenta as possible
  • Use oxytocics to control bleeding

Total Placenta Accreta
  • Complete family: Perform hysterectomy
  • Incomplete family:
    • Leave the placenta for autolysis within the uterus and administer antibiotics
    • Consider uterine artery embolisation or Methotrexate therapy

Placenta Percreta with Bladder Invasion

Perform hysterectomy with partial cystectomy.

 

Possible complications of PAS surgery:

  • Blood loss and need for immediate blood transfusion
  • Placental ingrowth to the bladder causes bleeding on attempting manual removal
  • Postoperative venous thromboembolism

The need for blood transfusion (Option B) is due to significant bleeding, which is a substantial risk in cases of PAS due to abnormal placental attachment.

The risk of requiring a hysterectomy (Option C) is a crucial aspect to discuss in counselling, as PAS cases often involve difficulty separating the placenta from the uterine wall, leading to potential complications that may necessitate a hysterectomy.

The risk of bladder injury (Option D) is a significant consideration in PAS cases. Abnormal placental attachment can lead to invasion into the bladder wall, increasing the risk of injury during attempts to separate the placenta from the uterine wall.

questions.stem: A 42-year-old female presents with complaints of recurrent episodes of abdominal pain and cramps. An endoscopy is done and she is diagnosed with ulcerative colitis. She currently has 3-4 episodes of bloody stools per day. What is the appropriate initial treatment?
questions.stemHtml: A 42-year-old female presents with complaints of recurrent episodes of abdominal pain and cramps. An endoscopy is done and she is diagnosed with ulcerative colitis. She currently has 3-4 episodes of bloody stools per day. What is the appropriate initial treatment?
questions.solution: pan> Explanation: Sulfasalazine is commonly used in the treatment of ulcerative colitis (inflammatory bowel disease). Sulfasalazine Anti-inflammatory Properties: Sulfasalazine is composed of two components: Sulfapyridine and 5-aminosalicylic acid (5-ASA) . The 5-ASA component is responsible for the drug's anti-inflammatory effects. It inhibits the production of inflammatory mediators such as prostaglandins and leukotrienes, which play a role in the inflammation seen in ulcerative colitis. Immunomodulatory Effects: Sulfasalazine also has immunomodulatory effects, which help to regulate the immune response in the gastrointestinal tract. By modulating the activity of immune cells such as macrophages and T cells, sulfasalazine can reduce inflammation. Antibacterial Activity: Sulfasalazine's sulfapyridine component has antibacterial properties. It acts by disrupting the metabolism of certain bacteria, particularly those in the gut microbiota. By targeting bacteria, sulfasalazine may help to restore balance to the gut microbiome. Local Action in the Colon: Sulfasalazine is administered orally, and its 5-ASA component is not absorbed systemically to a significant extent. Instead, it remains largely in the colon, where it exerts its anti-inflammatory effects directly on the inflamed tissue. This targeted action reduces the risk of systemic side effects commonly associated with corticosteroids or other systemic immunosuppressive agents. Maintenance Therapy: Sulfasalazine is often used as maintenance therapy in ulcerative colitis. It helps prevent flare-ups and maintain remission over the long term. Symptomatic Relief: In addition to its disease-modifying effects, sulfasalazine can provide symptomatic relief from the symptoms of ulcerative colitis, such as diarrhoea, abdominal pain, and rectal bleeding. Incorrect Options: Budesonide (Option A) is used in cases of exacerbation of ulcerative colitis, especially mild to moderate cases. Azathioprine (AZA) (Option C) is a medication used in the management and treatment of active rheumatoid arthritis (RA) and the prevention of kidney transplant rejection. Bezlotoxumab (Option D) is indicated to reduce the recurrence of Clostridium difficile infection (CDI) in patients who are receiving antibacterial drug treatment for CDI and are at high risk for CDI recurrence. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.answerText: Proceed with emergency LSCS (Lower Segment Cesarean Section)
questions.solution: presentation, and since the baby is term and the cervix is not fully dilated , the best management for this case is to proceed to cesarean section as definitive management. Cord presentation involves the umbilical cord being felt below the presenting part without membrane rupture. Both cord prolapse and cord presentation are obstetric emergencies, and the management is immediate delivery by emergency LSCS. The presenting part can be elevated to relieve cord compression (positional or with fingers if possible) till delivery is started or if the patient needs to be transferred. Management of cord prolapse is based on: Baby's status (living or dead) Baby's maturity Degree Living baby Definitive treatment Cesarean Section (Best option for mature, living babies) If immediate Safe Vaginal Delivery Possible: Head Engaged: Complete delivery with forceps (ventouse is less ideal). Breech Presentation: Complete delivery by breech extraction. If immediate Safe Vaginal Delivery Not Possible Minimise cord pressure until definitive treatment or transfer to a suitable hospital. Stop any ongoing oxytocin infusion. Bladder Filling: Use a Foley catheter to fill the bladder with 400–750 mL fluid—empty the bladder before cesarean delivery. Postural Treatment: Use an elevated Sims position with a pillow or wedge Cord Replacement: Place the cord back into the vagina to reduce vasospasm. Baby Dead Allow labour to proceed for spontaneous delivery. Rupturing the membranes (Option A) in this situation can lead to cord prolapse, which is a serious obstetric emergency. It is not advisable to intentionally rupture the membranes without a clear assessment and appropriate management plan. Oxytocin (Option B) is not the immediate solution in the presence of a prolapsed cord. The focus should be on relieving pressure on the cord and expediting delivery through emergency LSCS rather than initiating labor augmentation. She has a blind-ended vagina and clitoromegaly with normal testosterone levels. Her genotype is 46 XY. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A 15-year-old girl child with primary amenorrhea and signs of virilisation. She has prepubertal development of breasts and pubic hair and is tanner stage 2. She has a blind-ended vagina and clitoromegaly with normal testosterone levels. Her genotype is 46 XY. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.solution: dictid="209b85faf71692777185767d43e3bd">deficiency Explanation: The presentation of primary amenorrhea with virilisation, clitoromegaly, blind-ended vagina, and Tanner stage 2 pubic hair development, alongside a 46 XY genotype, suggests 5-alpha reductase deficiency. Definition: 5-alpha reductase deficiency is a condition with a deficiency in the enzyme 5-alpha reductase , which converts testosterone to dihydrotestosterone (DHT) . Features: DHT is crucial for the development of male external genitalia. Individuals with this deficiency typically have normal testosterone levels because the enzyme defect doesn't affect testosterone production. At birth, they are often assigned female because they have ambiguous genitalia or appear female externally. During puberty, testosterone levels increase, leading to virilization (e.g., clitoromegaly) They usually have a blind-ending vagina and often prepubertal breast development because DHT is important for male genital development but not for pubic hair development, which relies on testosterone. 17 hydroxylase deficiency (Option A) leads to impaired production of both sex steroids and cortisol, with accumulation of precursor steroids, leading to increased mineralocorticoid activity (hypertension and hypokalemia). Patients have ambiguous genitalia or female external genitalia due to low androgen levels, and the characteristic features include hypertension and hypokalemia. Normal testosterone levels would not be expected in 17 hydroxylase deficiency, which makes this option incorrect. Swyer syndrome (Option B) is a type of pure gonadal dysgenesis where individuals have a 46 XY karyotype but develop as females with streak gonads. They present with primary amenorrhea and underdeveloped secondary sexual characteristics (such as prepubertal breasts) and do not develop pubic hair due to a lack of sex steroid production, which is not the case given here. Complete AIS (Androgen Insensitivity Syndrome) (Option D) involves resistance to androgens in individuals with a 46 XY karyotype and typically have normal breast development due to aromatization of androgens to estrogens, no pubic or axillary hair (because of androgen resistance), and a blind-ending vagina. The presence of pubic hair and prepubertal breasts is not consistent with complete AIS @Neet_pg_bot

dictid="209b85faf71692777185767d43e3bd">deficiency

Explanation:

The presentation of primary amenorrhea with virilisation, clitoromegaly, blind-ended vagina, and Tanner stage 2 pubic hair development, alongside a 46 XY genotype, suggests 5-alpha reductase deficiency.

 

Definition:

5-alpha reductase deficiency is a condition with a deficiency in the enzyme 5-alpha reductase, which converts testosterone to dihydrotestosterone (DHT).

Features:

  • DHT is crucial for the development of male external genitalia.
  • Individuals with this deficiency typically have normal testosterone levels because the enzyme defect doesn't affect testosterone production.
  • At birth, they are often assigned female because they have ambiguous genitalia or appear female externally.
  • During puberty, testosterone levels increase, leading to virilization (e.g., clitoromegaly)
  • They usually have a blind-ending vagina and often prepubertal breast development because DHT is important for male genital development but not for pubic hair development, which relies on testosterone.

 

17 hydroxylase deficiency (Option A) leads to impaired production of both sex steroids and cortisol, with accumulation of precursor steroids, leading to increased mineralocorticoid activity (hypertension and hypokalemia). Patients have ambiguous genitalia or female external genitalia due to low androgen levels, and the characteristic features include hypertension and hypokalemia. Normal testosterone levels would not be expected in 17 hydroxylase deficiency, which makes this option incorrect.

Swyer syndrome (Option B) is a type of pure gonadal dysgenesis where individuals have a 46 XY karyotype but develop as females with streak gonads. They present with primary amenorrhea and underdeveloped secondary sexual characteristics (such as prepubertal breasts) and do not develop pubic hair due to a lack of sex steroid production, which is not the case given here.

Complete AIS (Androgen Insensitivity Syndrome) (Option D) involves resistance to androgens in individuals with a 46 XY karyotype and typically have normal breast development due to aromatization of androgens to estrogens, no pubic or axillary hair (because of androgen resistance), and a blind-ending vagina. The presence of pubic hair and prepubertal breasts is not consistent with complete AIS

  • Head and neck lymphadenopathy
  • Conjunctivitis
  • Spontaneous abortions
  • Devastating fetal infections

Fetal features

  • 13 to 14 gestation: 50% incidence of an affected fetus
  • End of 2nd trimester: 25%
  • After 20 weeks: Defects are rare

Diagnosis

  • Urine analysis
  • Blood analysis
  • Nasopharyngeal secretions
  • CSF analysis
  • ELISA: Specific IgM antibody

Management and prevention

  • Droplet precautions for 7 days after onset of rash
  • Postexposure passive immunization with IVIG within 5 days of exposure
  • MMR vaccine to non-pregnant women of childbearing age
  • Targeted USG to determine fetal anomalies in infected mothers
  • Vaccination of all susceptible hospital personnel

 

Hepatitis B (Option A) transmission transplacentally is uncommon but vertical transmission is seen by exposure to blood or other bodily fluids during birth. All pregnant mothers are screened at the beginning of the pregnancy, and if found positive, the newborns are given hepatitis B immunoglobulin with a hepatitis B recombinant vaccine series.

In HSV (Option B), Fetal infection can occur by shedding of virus from the lower genital tract during vaginal delivery or rupture of membranes. Neonatal infection, when symptomatic, can present with chorioretinitis, mental retardation, microcephaly, seizures, and occasionally death.

CMV (Option D) is a DNA virus transmitted by sexual, respiratory droplets and transplacental route. Infection can affect the fetus throughout gestation and cause microcephaly, intracranial calcification, chorioretinitis, mental retardation, nonimmune hydrops, stillbirth, IUGR, hepatosplenomegaly, thrombocytopenia, and sensorineural deafness. Transmission is more common in the third trimester and during delivery.

questions.solutionHtml:
trong>Explanation:
  • The scenario here is of Addisonian crisis (or adrenal crisis) that was triggered due to the abrupt cessation of medications for rheumatoid arthritis (glucocorticoids like prednisone). This is treated with intravenous hydrocortisone.

Clinical features of adrenal crisis
  • Circulatory shock
  • Severe hypotension
  • Hyponatremia
  • Hyperkalemia
  • Hypoglycemia
  • Hypercalcemia
  • Muscle cramps
  • Nausea
  • Vomiting
  • Diarrhea
  • Unexplained fever

Precipitating factors:

  • Other illnesses
  • Surgery
  • Infection

Management of adrenal crisis:

  • Correct volume depletion
    • IV saline for correcting blood pressure and pulse
  • Replace glucocorticoids
    • IV hydrocortisone succinate 100 mg stat and 100 mg QID for first 12-24 hrs
    • Parenteral hydrocortisone 50-100 mg IM QID till the patient can take it orally
  • Correct metabolic abnormalities
    • Acute hypoglycemia: IV 10% glucose
    • Hyperkalemia: Usually corrected with volume replacement, otherwise needs specific treatment
  • Identify and treat the underlying cause
    • Acute precipitating factors like infection
    • Adrenal or pituitary pathology

Incorrect Options:

Fast IV fluids (Option A) is one of the steps in management to correct the blood pressure and pulse but it is not the definitive treatment for Addisonian crisis which needs to be managed with IV hydrocortisone.

Dopamine infusion (Option C) is not a definitive treatment for adrenal crisis and is used to treat low blood pressure, low heart rate, and cardiac arrest.

Soda bicarbonate (Option D) is not indicated for adrenal crisis.

Cystocele

Clinical features
  • Urinary incontinence
  • Pelvic discomfort
  • Anterior vaginal wall prolapse
  • Bulge shows transverse rugosities and impulse on coughing

Management

Surgical: (recommended for women >40 years)

  • Anterior Colporrhaphy: (most preferred)
    • weakened tissue between the bladder and vagina is repaired.
  • Mesh Repair:
    • synthetic mesh is used for additional support.
    • Risk of recurrence, mesh erosion and infection
  • Sacral Colpopexy:
    • Mesh is attached from the top of the vagina to the sacrum to lift the prolapsed organs.
    • High risk of recurrence and complications
  • Vaginal Hysterectomy:
    • Considered in cases where uterine prolapse coexists with cystocele.

Conservative:

  • Recommended in young women with prolapse following childbirth for the initial 4-6 months
  • Pelvic floor exercises
  • Lifestyle modifications: Avoid heavy lifting and constipation
  • Pessary insertion (in patients unfit for surgery)

 

Hysterectomy (Option A) involves the removal of the uterus and is a common treatment for uterine prolapse, especially when conservative measures fail to provide relief and in women older than 40 years.

Sacrospinous fixation or sacrospinous colpopexy (Option B) can fix the vaginal vault to sacrospinous ligaments. Vault prolapse is a delayed complication of hysterectomy. This is the preferred treatment for vault prolapse.

The surgical treatment of rectocele is posterior colporrhaphy or colpoperineorrhaphy (Option C). Protrusion of the rectum with the posterior vaginal wall is called rectocele.

questions.solution: 3,3′-Diaminobenzidine (DAB) is a commonly used chromogen in immunohistochemistry (IHC) to detect HER2 overexpression in certain breast cancers. It serves as a substrate for a peroxidase enzyme coupled to a primary or secondary antibody. It is oxidised and converted to an insoluble polymer, precipitating as a dark brown pigment, which allows visualisation of the target molecule. FITC (Fluorescein Isothiocyanate) (Option A) is a fluorescent dye that is used in fluorescence microscopy to detect specific antigens but does not produce a brown colour. Cyanate dye (Option C) is commonly used in fluorescence-based applications such as fluorescent labelling of biomolecules in biological and biochemical research. Immune Reconstitution Syndrome : Occurs after initiating effective ART, leading to worsening of pre-existing opportunistic infections or autoimmune conditions. Types of IRIS: Paradoxical IRIS: Exacerbation of known pre-existing infections or neoplasms. Unmasking IRIS: Emergence of previously undiagnosed conditions. Immune Reconstitution Disease (IRD) : Refers to IRIS related to opportunistic infections or autoimmune diseases. Symptoms : Lymphadenitis Prolonged fever Pulmonary infiltrates Hepatitis Increased intracranial pressure Uveitis Sarcoidosis Graves’ disease Mechanism : Related to type IV hypersensitivity reactions due to immune recovery as HIV RNA levels drop and immune suppression is reversed. Management : Severe cases may require immunosuppressive drugs (e.g., glucocorticoids) alongside specific antimicrobial therapy. fungal treatment

Explanation:
  • The patient has signs and symptoms of meningitis, which, along with the positive India ink stain leads to the diagnosis of Cryptococcal meningitis, which is a CNS complication of HIV occurring due to opportunistic infection by Cryptococcus neoformans.

 

Fungal Meningitis in AIDS

  • The leading cause of meningitis in AIDS patients is primarily Cryptococcus neoformans (C. neoformans), with C. gattii accounting for up to 12% of cases.
  • Cryptococcal meningitis is common in patients with CD4+ T-cell counts <100/μL, especially in untreated AIDS patients.

Symptoms:

  • Subacute meningoencephalitis with fever, nausea, vomiting, altered mental status, headache, and meningeal signs
  • Seizures and focal neurologic deficits are rare
  • Elevated intracranial pressure (Option A)

CSF Findings:

  • Mild increase in WBCs and protein
  • Low glucose
  • Elevated opening pressure

Diagnosis:

  • CSF: Positive India ink examination
  • Cryptococcal antigen detection in CSF
  • Blood cultures may also be positive
  • A biopsy may be needed for CNS cryptococcoma or distinguishing from immune reconstitution syndrome
  • MRI: Soap bubble appearance is seen in less than 30% of cases (Option D)

 

Treatment:

  • Initial: IV Amphotericin B with Flucytosine for at least 2 weeks. (Option C)
  • Continued with Amphotericin until CSF culture is negative, followed by Fluconazole (400 mg/d) for 8 weeks and then 200 mg/d until CD4+ T-cell count >200/μL for 6 months.
  • Repeated lumbar punctures may be needed to manage elevated intracranial pressure.

 

Immune Reconstitution Syndrome:

  • Occurs after initiating effective ART, leading to worsening of pre-existing opportunistic infections or autoimmune conditions.
  • Types of IRIS:
    • Paradoxical IRIS: Exacerbation of known pre-existing infections or neoplasms.
    • Unmasking IRIS: Emergence of previously undiagnosed conditions.
    • Immune Reconstitution Disease (IRD): Refers to IRIS related to opportunistic infections or autoimmune diseases.
  • Symptoms:
    • Lymphadenitis
    • Prolonged fever
    • Pulmonary infiltrates
    • Hepatitis
    • Increased intracranial pressure
    • Uveitis
    • Sarcoidosis
    • Graves’ disease
  • Mechanism: Related to type IV hypersensitivity reactions due to immune recovery as HIV RNA levels drop and immune suppression is reversed.
  • Management:
    • Severe cases may require immunosuppressive drugs (e.g., glucocorticoids) alongside specific antimicrobial therapy.
    • Due to the risk of IRIS (immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome), ART should be deferred by 4-6 weeks after the initiation of antifungal treatment.

 

Other Causes:

  • Other fungi like C. immitis and H. capsulatum, as well as amoebas like Acanthamoeba and Naegleria, can cause meningitis in HIV-infected individuals.

questions.solutionHtml:
strong>Explanation:

The true association of hormone replacement therapy is with a decreased risk of colon cancer.

Hormone replacement therapy

  • This is used for the treatment of menopausal symptoms
  • They are usually estrogen and occasionally in combination with progesterone
  • HRT decreases the risk of colon cancer due to the protective effects of estrogen
  • Hence, the incidence of colon cancer is rare amongst women of reproductive age group compared to men of the same age group

Indications of HRT:

  • Therapeutic:
    • Symptomatic menopausal women
    • Gonadal dysgenesis in adolescents
  • Prophylactic:
  • Patients at high risk for menopausal complications like cardiovascular disease, osteoporosis, stroke, colon cancer, etc
  • Premature menopause: Spontaneous following surgery or cancer therapy

 

Breast cancer risk (Option A) is increased by hyperestrogenism. Breast cancer following HRT is usually low-grade and shows a good prognosis.

Estrogen replacement (Option B) can increase the risk of well-differentiated endometrial carcinoma. The addition of progesterone to estrogen reduces the risk of endometrial cancer.

After menopause, bone density decreases every year, leading to osteopenia and, eventually, osteoporosis (Option C). Osteoporosis would usually result in fractures of vertebrae, femur and wrist. HRT using estrogen protects against osteoporosis and decreases the risk of fractures.

questions.stem: A patient on amitriptyline was discovered unconscious at home and potentially suspected of TCA toxicity. Which of the following features is less commonly associated with TCA toxicity?
questions.stemHtml: A patient on amitriptyline was discovered unconscious at home and potentially suspected of TCA toxicity. Which of the following features is less commonly associated with TCA toxicity?
questions.solution: Correct Option C - Hypothermia: Amitriptyline is a Tricyclic Antidepressant (TCA) that can cause hyperthermia as a side effect rather than hypothermia. Side effects of Tricyclic antidepressants (TCA): Mechanism of side effect Side effect H1 receptor blockade Sedation, weight gain Anticholinergic action on muscarinic receptors Hyperthermia (Option C) Dry eyes/mouth Mydriasis (C/I in glaucoma) (Option D ruled out) Urinary retention Constipation Tachycardia Confusion (Option B ruled out) Increase in serotonin in the brain Seizure threshold reduction Alpha 1 adrenergic receptor antagonism Postural hypotension Sodium channel block Arrhythmia/QT prolongation (Option A ruled out) Bradycardia in heart block due to overdose TCA poisoning Poisoning with TCAs is frequent, usually self-attempted for suicide, and may endanger life. Manifestations are Excitement, delirium and other anticholinergic symptoms, as seen in atropine poisoning, followed by muscle spasms, convulsions and coma. Respiration is depressed, body temperature may fall, low BP, and prominent tachycardia. ECG changes and ventricular arrhythmias are common. Treatment Primarily supportive with gastric lavage, respiratory assistance, fluid infusion, maintenance of BP and body temperature. Acidosis must be corrected by bicarbonate infusion. Diazepam may be injected I.V. to control convulsions and delirium. Most important is treating cardiac arrhythmias, for which propranolol/ lidocaine may be used. The class IA and IC antiarrhythmics and digoxin depress cardiac conduction; therefore, they are contraindicated. @Neet_pg_bot

Correct Option C - Hypothermia:

  • Amitriptyline is a Tricyclic Antidepressant (TCA) that can cause hyperthermia as a side effect rather than hypothermia.

Side effects of Tricyclic antidepressants (TCA):

Mechanism of side effect

Side effect

H1 receptor blockade
  • Sedation, weight gain

Anticholinergic action on muscarinic receptors
  • Hyperthermia (Option C)
  • Dry eyes/mouth
  • Mydriasis (C/I in glaucoma) (Option D ruled out)
  • Urinary retention
  • Constipation
  • Tachycardia
  • Confusion (Option B ruled out)

Increase in serotonin in the brain

Alpha 1 adrenergic receptor antagonism
