questions.stem: In which of the following conditions is live vaccination not contraindicated? DiGeorge syndrome Wiskott Aldrich Syndrome Ataxia telangiectasia Complement deficiency
questions.stemHtml:
In which of the following conditions is live vaccination not contraindicated?
	DiGeorge syndrome
	Wiskott Aldrich Syndrome
	Ataxia telangiectasia
	Complement deficiency
questions.solution: ation: Live vaccines are typically contraindicated in conditions associated with impaired T-cell immunity, as individuals with such deficiencies are at risk for severe infections due to their inability to mount an adequate immune response to live pathogens. This includes DiGeorge syndrome, Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome, and Ataxia telangiectasia. In contrast, patients with complement deficiencies have normal T-cell and B-cell functions. They may have an increased susceptibility to certain bacterial infections, particularly those caused by Neisseria species, due to defective complement-mediated immunity. However, their adaptive immune system, which is responsible for responding to vaccines, remains intact. Therefore, live vaccinations are generally not contraindicated in complement deficiency. DiGeorge syndrome (1) involves a defect in the development of the thymus, leading to T-cell deficiency and impaired cell-mediated immunity. As a result, live vaccines should be avoided due to the increased risk of severe infections. Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome (2) is caused by mutations in the Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome protein (WASP), leading to T-cell dysfunction. Live vaccines are contraindicated in these patients because of their compromised immune system. Ataxia telangiectasia (3) results from mutations in the ATM gene, impairing DNA repair mechanisms and leading to T-cell deficiency. Live vaccines are avoided due to the risk of severe infection. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: An 18-month-old child with a 3-day history of watery diarrhea and vomiting presented with altered sensorium. Which of the following are differential diagnoses? Severe dehydration Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (HUS) Cerebral Venous Thrombosis Hyponatremia
questions.stemHtml:
An 18-month-old child with a 3-day history of watery diarrhea and vomiting presented with altered sensorium. Which of the following are differential diagnoses?
	Severe dehydration
	Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (HUS)
	Cerebral Venous Thrombosis
	Hyponatremia
questions.solution: In a child presenting with diarrhea, vomiting, and altered sensorium, the differential diagnosis should focus on conditions associated with metabolic derangements, dehydration, and potential neurological complications. Severe Dehydration (1): Prolonged diarrhea and vomiting can lead to hypovolemia and electrolyte imbalances, resulting in altered sensorium. This is one of the most common causes of altered mental status in children with diarrheal illness. Cerebral Venous Thrombosis (CVT) (3): Severe dehydration increases the risk of thrombosis due to hemoconcentration. CVT can present with seizures, altered sensorium, and focal neurological signs. Hyponatremia (4): Excessive water intake or inappropriate antidiuretic hormone (ADH) release in response to dehydration can cause dilutional hyponatremia. Symptoms include seizures, lethargy, and altered sensorium. Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (HUS) (2): This condition is typically associated with bloody diarrhea, which is absent in the clinical presentation. HUS is caused by Shiga toxin-producing E. coli and usually occurs several days after an initial diarrheal illness. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
In a child presenting with diarrhea, vomiting, and altered sensorium, the differential diagnosis should focus on conditions associated with metabolic derangements, dehydration, and potential neurological complications.

 

Severe Dehydration (1):

  • Prolonged diarrhea and vomiting can lead to hypovolemia and electrolyte imbalances, resulting in altered sensorium.
  • This is one of the most common causes of altered mental status in children with diarrheal illness.

 

Cerebral Venous Thrombosis (CVT) (3):

  • Severe dehydration increases the risk of thrombosis due to hemoconcentration.
  • CVT can present with seizures, altered sensorium, and focal neurological signs.

 

Hyponatremia (4):

  • Excessive water intake or inappropriate antidiuretic hormone (ADH) release in response to dehydration can cause dilutional hyponatremia.
  • Symptoms include seizures, lethargy, and altered sensorium.

 

Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (HUS) (2):

  • This condition is typically associated with bloody diarrhea, which is absent in the clinical presentation.
  • HUS is caused by Shiga toxin-producing E. coli and usually occurs several days after an initial diarrheal illness.

questions.solution: 3c65a0c79f1">MRCP (Magnetic Resonance Cholangiopancreatography) image reveals dilation of the common bile duct (CBD) along with filling defects, representing gallstones within the duct. Filling defects on MRCP indicate an obstruction in the bile ducts, commonly caused by gallstones (choledocholithiasis) or other blockages. These defects appear as areas where the bile duct does not fill properly or has reduced signal intensity. Symptoms of choledocholithiasis typically include jaundice, abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. Treatment often involves endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) with sphincterotomy and stone extraction. Incorrect Options: Stricture (Option A) : A bile duct stricture appears as narrowing or constriction of the bile duct caused by inflammation, scarring, or tumours obstructing the duct. While it can mimic choledocholithiasis on imaging, it does not show the characteristic filling defects seen in choledocholithiasis. Cholecystitis (Option C) is the inflammation of the gallbladder, usually due to gallstones blocking the cystic duct. MRCP typically shows gallbladder wall thickening, pericholecystic fluid, and gallstones in the gallbladder but not changes in the bile ducts, so it wouldn't cause CBD dilation or filling defects. Cholangiocarcinoma (Option D) is a malignant tumour of the bile duct epithelium. On MRCP, it can cause bile duct dilation and strictures and may also show intraductal masses or nodules. However, the pattern of obstruction caused by a tumour differs from the filling defects seen with choledocholithiasis, as these defects are caused by gallstones, not a mass. @Neet_pg_bot

  • Symptoms of choledocholithiasis typically include jaundice, abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting.
  • Treatment often involves endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) with sphincterotomy and stone extraction.

 

Incorrect Options:

Stricture (Option A): A bile duct stricture appears as narrowing or constriction of the bile duct caused by inflammation, scarring, or tumours obstructing the duct. While it can mimic choledocholithiasis on imaging, it does not show the characteristic filling defects seen in choledocholithiasis.

Cholecystitis (Option C) is the inflammation of the gallbladder, usually due to gallstones blocking the cystic duct. MRCP typically shows gallbladder wall thickening, pericholecystic fluid, and gallstones in the gallbladder but not changes in the bile ducts, so it wouldn't cause CBD dilation or filling defects.

Cholangiocarcinoma (Option D) is a malignant tumour of the bile duct epithelium. On MRCP, it can cause bile duct dilation and strictures and may also show intraductal masses or nodules. However, the pattern of obstruction caused by a tumour differs from the filling defects seen with choledocholithiasis, as these defects are caused by gallstones, not a mass.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy presents with a history of fever, conjunctival congestion, and erythematous desquamation of the skin. A 2D echocardiogram shows coronary aneurysms. What is the first-line treatment for this condition?
questions.stemHtml: A 4-year-old boy presents with a history of fever, conjunctival congestion, and erythematous desquamation of the skin. A 2D echocardiogram shows coronary aneurysms. What is the first-line treatment for this condition?
questions.solution: —fever, conjunctival congestion, strawberry tongue, and erythematous desquamation—along with coronary aneurysms on echocardiography, is highly suggestive of Kawasaki disease (mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome). The first-line treatment is intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) combined with aspirin, aimed at reducing inflammation and preventing coronary artery complications. Kawasaki Disease (KD) Etiology and Pathophysiology Higher incidence in children of Asian descent. Vasculitis affecting medium-sized arteries, especially coronary arteries. Pathology Acute Phase (Days 1-10): Neutrophilic inflammation of blood vessels. Infiltration of inflammatory cells, vessel wall swelling and damage. Subacute Phase (Weeks 2-4): Risk of fusiform aneurysm formation as inflammation subsides. Convalescent Phase (Weeks >4 weeks): Resolution of inflammation; potential scarring and thickening of arterial walls leading to stenosis. Clinical Features Fever : For at least 5 days. Extremities: Swelling, redness, peeling skin around nails, fingers, and toes. Mucocutaneous: Bilateral conjunctivitis, red and cracked lips, "strawberry tongue," and pharyngeal congestion. Polymorphous Rash : Various forms (macular, papular, target-like lesions). Cervical Lymphadenopathy : Unilateral, painful swelling of neck lymph nodes. Diagnosis Clinical Criteria: Fever lasting at least 5 days. At least 4 of the following: 5-“ CREAM” features C - Conjunctivitis, B/L non-purulent R - Rash involving trunk E- Erythema & Edema of palms & soles along with desquamation A - Adenopathy (usually unilateral, cervical) M- Mucositis (Strawberry Tongue) Laboratory Findings: Elevated CRP and ESR. Elevated WBC count. Echocardiography coronary artery aneurysms. Complications Myocardial infarction. Coronary Artery Aneurysms. Coronary Artery Stenosis: Differential Diagnosis Bacterial Infections (e.g., Scarlet Fever, Staphylococcal Scalded Skin Syndrome): Fever, rash, mucosal involvement with additional features like sore throat or blistering. Treatment Intravenous Immunoglobulin (IVIG): Reduces inflammation and lowers risk of aneurysms. Aspirin: High doses initially to reduce inflammation and fever; then low-dose regimen for anti-platelet effects. IVIG-Resistant KD: Second dose of IVIG, corticosteroids, or other immunosuppressive medications (e.g., infliximab, cyclosporine). Aspirin (Option A): Important in treatment but is not the first-line therapy alone. It complements IVIG to control inflammation and reduce thrombotic risks. Clopidogrel (Option C): Antiplatelet agent used for specific coronary conditions but not a primary treatment for Kawasaki disease. LMWH (Low Molecular Weight Heparin) (Option D): Used in cases with significant thrombotic complications but not first-line therapy. @Neet_pg_bot

  • Fever: For at least 5 days.
  • Extremities: Swelling, redness, peeling skin around nails, fingers, and toes.
  • Mucocutaneous: Bilateral conjunctivitis, red and cracked lips, "strawberry tongue," and pharyngeal congestion.
  • Polymorphous Rash: Various forms (macular, papular, target-like lesions).
  • Cervical Lymphadenopathy: Unilateral, painful swelling of neck lymph nodes.

Diagnosis

Clinical Criteria:

 

Fever lasting at least 5 days.

 

At least 4 of the following:

 

5-“CREAM” features

 

  • C - Conjunctivitis, B/L non-purulent
  • R - Rash involving trunk
  • E- Erythema & Edema of palms & soles along with desquamation
  • A - Adenopathy (usually unilateral, cervical)
  • M- Mucositis (Strawberry Tongue)

 

Laboratory Findings:

  • Elevated CRP and ESR.
  • Elevated WBC count.
  • Echocardiography coronary artery aneurysms.

Complications
  • Myocardial infarction.
  • Coronary Artery Aneurysms.
  • Coronary Artery Stenosis:

Differential Diagnosis

Bacterial Infections (e.g., Scarlet Fever, Staphylococcal Scalded Skin Syndrome): Fever, rash, mucosal involvement with additional features like sore throat or blistering.

Treatment
  • Intravenous Immunoglobulin (IVIG): Reduces inflammation and lowers risk of aneurysms.
  • Aspirin: High doses initially to reduce inflammation and fever; then low-dose regimen for anti-platelet effects.

 

IVIG-Resistant KD:

  • Second dose of IVIG, corticosteroids, or other immunosuppressive medications (e.g., infliximab, cyclosporine).

 

Aspirin (Option A): Important in treatment but is not the first-line therapy alone. It complements IVIG to control inflammation and reduce thrombotic risks.

Clopidogrel (Option C): Antiplatelet agent used for specific coronary conditions but not a primary treatment for Kawasaki disease.

LMWH (Low Molecular Weight Heparin) (Option D): Used in cases with significant thrombotic complications but not first-line therapy.

ions, caudal regression is not associated with Down syndrome. Caudal regression is a condition characterized by the abnormal development of the lower spine and limbs, and it is more frequently seen in infants of diabetic mothers rather than those with Down syndrome.

Down's Syndrome (Trisomy 21)

 

Cause
  • Trisomy 21 due to meiotic nondisjunction.
  • Less commonly caused by Robertsonian translocation (4%) or mosaicism (1%).

Incidence

1:800 to 1:1000 live births.

General Features

Craniofacial:

  • Intellectual disability, flat facial profile, upward-slanting eyes, epicanthic folds.
  • Small nose, flat nasal bridge, narrow palate, small teeth, protruding tongue.
  • Brachycephaly, flat occiput, dysplastic ears.

 

Extremities:

  • Short, broad hands, clinodactyly (5th finger), simian crease, sandal gap (wide space between toes).

Comorbidities

Cardiac: 40-60% have congenital heart defects (mainly AVSD, VSD, PDA, ASD).

Gastrointestinal: Duodenal atresia, Hirschsprung disease, annular pancreas.

Hematological: Increased risk of leukemia (acute lymphoblastic leukemia, acute myeloid leukemia).

Endocrine: Thyroid dysfunction (hypothyroidism), type 1 diabetes risk.

Neurological: Early-onset Alzheimer’s disease (APP gene on chromosome 21).

Musculoskeletal: Atlanto-occipital subluxation, short stature, hypotonia, growth delays, obesity risk.

Sensory: Hearing loss (conductive, often due to serous otitis media), ophthalmic problems (cataracts, strabismus, nystagmus).

Diagnosis

Prenatal:

  • Chorionic Villus Sampling (CVS): Performed between 10-13 weeks.
  • Amniocentesis: Performed after 15 weeks.

Postnatal:

  • Characteristic features (e.g., craniofacial dysmorphisms).
  • Confirmatory Test: Karyotype analysis for trisomy 21.

Antenatal Screening

First Trimester: Increased nuchal translucency (>3 mm), elevated β-HCG, low PAPP-A.

Second Trimester: Triple Test (β-HCG, estriol, AFP), Quadruple Test (adds Inhibin-A).

Integrated Test: Combines maternal age, NT, PAPP-A, and Quadruple Test.

Non-Invasive Prenatal Testing (NIPS/NIPT): Cell-free fetal DNA testing (high sensitivity and specificity).

questions.stem: A surgeon examines a case of hernia and is able to retract the hernial sac but not its contents. Based on this examination, which type of hernia is most likely?
questions.stemHtml: A surgeon examines a case of hernia and is able to retract the hernial sac but not its contents. Based on this examination, which type of hernia is most likely?
questions.solution: /p> Reduction en masse refers to the unintentional displacement or reduction of both the hernia sac and its contents into a deeper anatomical space, such as the preperitoneal or retroperitoneal space, which can occur during the attempted reduction of the hernia. Incorrect Options: Incarcerated hernia (Option A) : In an incarcerated hernia , the lumen of the part of the colon within the hernial sac becomes obstructed by faeces. The fecal content, or scybalous material, can typically be indented with a finger, similar to putty. In this condition, the sac and its contents are firmly adhered to each other, meaning the contents are fixed within the sac. The hernia is always irreducible and often obstructed, though it may not necessarily be strangulated. Sliding hernia (Hernia-En-Glissade) (Option C) : It occurs when a portion of the peritoneum that normally lines the abdominal cavity slides through the hernia defect, bringing a partially retroperitoneal organ. It is more common in males, particularly the elderly and frequently occurs on the left side , where the sigmoid colon is the most common content, not the appendix. The posterior wall of the hernia sac is formed by the viscera (commonly bowel), not the anterior wall. Clinical presentation: Patients typically present with a reducible swelling in the groin or lower abdomen that worsens on standing due to gravity. Gastrointestinal symptoms like constipation and incomplete bowel emptying are common, indicating bowel involvement. Managed surgically by repairing or closing the defect , but associated with a higher risk of bowel injury due to the involvement of the viscera in the hernia sac. Maydl’s Hernia: {{caption_text}} It involves two or more bowel loops that become incarcerated or strangulated within the hernia sac. The obstructed loop is present intraperitoneally and easily missed during surgery. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Among the options provided, which one is NOT acknowledged as a potential complication resulting from a significant blood transfusion?
questions.stemHtml: Among the options provided, which one is NOT acknowledged as a potential complication resulting from a significant blood transfusion?
questions.solution: Hypernatremia is not typically a complication of blood transfusion. Complications of massive blood transfusion: Hypocalcemia : (Option A) Packed red blood cells (PRBCs) and other blood products are preserved with citrate , an anticoagulant. Citrate binds to ionised calcium (Ca²⁺) in the recipient's blood, reducing the free calcium level - hypocalcemia. Presents as muscle spasms, cardiac arrhythmias, and decreased myocardial contractility. Metabolic Alkalosis : Citrate is metabolised in the liver to bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻) . Rapid transfusion of citrate-containing blood products can overwhelm the liver’s ability to metabolise citrate, leading to an increase in bicarbonate levels. This results in metabolic alkalosis Hyperkalemia : Stored blood undergoes hemolysis over time, releasing potassium from red blood cells into the plasma. Transfusion of large volumes of stored blood can introduce a significant potassium load, causing hyperkalemia . Presents with cardiac arrhythmias, especially in patients with pre-existing kidney dysfunction. Hypothermia : (Option C) Rapid transfusion of cold-stored blood products (typically kept at 1–6°C) can lower the patient’s core body temperature. Coagulopathy : Massive transfusion dilutes clotting factors and platelets, leading to dilutional coagulopathy . Hypothermia and hypocalcemia exacerbate this by impairing the function of coagulation enzymes and platelets. Hypokalemia : (Option B) Post-transfusion, potassium that had leaked out of stored red blood cells can re-enter the cells in vivo. This shift can lead to hypokalemia , especially if the patient has a strong cellular uptake of potassium. @Neet_pg_bot

    • Complications of massive blood transfusion:

    • Hypocalcemia: (Option A)
      • Packed red blood cells (PRBCs) and other blood products are preserved with citrate, an anticoagulant.
      • Citrate binds to ionised calcium (Ca²⁺) in the recipient's blood, reducing the free calcium level - hypocalcemia.
      • Presents as muscle spasms, cardiac arrhythmias, and decreased myocardial contractility.
    • Metabolic Alkalosis:
      • Citrate is metabolised in the liver to bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻).
      • Rapid transfusion of citrate-containing blood products can overwhelm the liver’s ability to metabolise citrate, leading to an increase in bicarbonate levels.
      • This results in metabolic alkalosis
    • Hyperkalemia:
      • Stored blood undergoes hemolysis over time, releasing potassium from red blood cells into the plasma.
      • Transfusion of large volumes of stored blood can introduce a significant potassium load, causing hyperkalemia.
      • Presents with cardiac arrhythmias, especially in patients with pre-existing kidney dysfunction.
    • Hypothermia: (Option C)
      • Rapid transfusion of cold-stored blood products (typically kept at 1–6°C) can lower the patient’s core body temperature.
    • Coagulopathy:
      • Massive transfusion dilutes clotting factors and platelets, leading to dilutional coagulopathy.
      • Hypothermia and hypocalcemia exacerbate this by impairing the function of coagulation enzymes and platelets.
    • Hypokalemia: (Option B)
      • Post-transfusion, potassium that had leaked out of stored red blood cells can re-enter the cells in vivo.
      • This shift can lead to hypokalemia, especially if the patient has a strong cellular uptake of potassium.

questions.solution: In the context of Breast Conservation Surgery (BCS) , Radiotherapy (RT) is Not optional but a necessary treatment component. Breast Conservation Therapy (BCT) combines BCS and post-operative radiotherapy (RT). All patients undergoing BCS will receive radiotherapy, which is integral to the treatment. The equation for this therapy is BCS + RT = BCT. Breast-conserving surgery (BCS) , also known as lumpectomy, involves removing a breast tumour along with a small margin of surrounding healthy tissue while preserving the majority of the breast. The goal is to remove the cancerous cells while maintaining the breast's appearance and function. Contraindications for Breast-Conserving Surgery (BCS): Absolute Contraindications First-trimester Pregnancy Multicentric Disease Diffuse Suspicious microcalcifications on mammogram Extensive DCIS Inflammatory Breast Cancer Tumors for which Clear Margins are Unobtainable with Lumpectomy Homozygous for ATM Mutation Relative Contraindications Prior Radiation Therapy to the Chest Wall or Breast Active Connective Tissue Disease Involving the Skin (e.g., Scleroderma) Extensive Positive Pathological Margins Large Tumor Size Relative to Breast Size or Tumors Greater Than 5 cm Known or Suspected Li-Fraumeni Syndrome (p53 Mutation) Known or Suspected Genetic Predisposition to Breast Cancer (e.g., BRCA1, BRCA2) @Neet_pg_bot

  • Posterior fixation of the rectum of Lockhardt-Mummery
  • Mickulicz Miles perineal transanal recto sigmoidectomy
  • Anal encircling (Thiersch) (Option C)

Advantages
  • Fixation of the rectum provides adequate tension to prevent recurrence.
  • Minimally invasive options (laparoscopic or robotic) offer benefits in pain control, hospital stay, and recovery time
  • Lower operative morbidity and mortality, suitable for elderly or medically unfit patients.

 

Disadvantages
  • Requires extensive dissection and fixation, which may have higher morbidity (10%-33%).
  • Risk of mesh-related complications such as erosion, infection, bowel obstruction, and migration.
  • Higher recurrence rates compared to abdominal approaches

questions.stem: All of the following drugs are used in the management of thyroid storm except:
questions.stemHtml: All of the following drugs are used in the management of thyroid storm except:
questions.solution: Correct Answer: D) Aspirin Aspirin is an antiplatelet drug that displaces thyroxine from thyroxine-binding globulin and increases free T3 and T4 levels ,which can be dangerous and worsen thyroid storm. Management of thyroid storm: Large doses of propylthiouracil (500–1000 mg loading dose and 250 mg every 4 h) should be given orally or by nasogastric tube or per rectum; the drug’s inhibitory action on T4 → T3 conversion makes it the antithyroid drug of choice. If not available, methimazole can be used in doses of 20 mg every 6 h. One hour after the first dose of propylthiouracil, stable iodide (5 drops SSKI every 6 h) is given to block thyroid hormone synthesis via the Wolff-Chaikoff effect (the delay allows the antithyroid drug to prevent the excess iodine from being incorporated into new hormone). Propranolol should also be given to reduce tachycardia and other adrenergic manifestations (60–80 mg PO every 4 h, or 2 mg IV every 4 h). Although other β-adrenergic blockers can be used, high doses of propranolol decrease T4 → T3 conversion, and the doses can be easily adjusted. Short-acting IV esmolol can be used to decrease heart rate while monitoring for signs of heart failure. Additional therapeutic measures include glucocorticoids (e.g., hydrocortisone 300 mg IV bolus, then 100 mg every 8 h), antibiotics if infection is present, cholestyramine to sequester thyroid hormones, cooling, oxygen, and IV fluids. Propranolol (Option A): Beta blockers are indicated to manage tachycardia in patients with thyroid storm. Lugol’s Iodine (Option B) inhibits further release of thyroxine. Propylthiouracil (Option C) inhibitsthe conversion of T4 to T3. @Neet_pg_bot

ly diagnosis is PTH adenoma. Parathyroid hormone (PTH) adenoma can cause hypercalcemia, which may lead to symptoms like dysuria and back pain. Radiologically, PTH adenoma may cause characteristic findings, such as kidney stones or calcifications due to calcium imbalance.

 

Causes of primary hyperparathyroidism :

  • The most common cause of primary hyperparathyroidism is a solitary parathyroid adenoma ( most common on the inferior lobe of the right parathyroid). Double adenomas are rare (2-4%).
  • Parathyroid hyperplasia: enlargement of all 4 glands.
  • Parathyroid carcinoma

Wilms' tumour (Option B) is a type of kidney cancer that predominantly affects children. It typically presents as a renal mass on imaging studies, but this would not be the correct diagnosis based on the provided X-ray image.

 

Renal cell carcinoma (Option C) is the most common form of kidney cancer in adults. While it may show up in imaging studies, an X-ray alone is insufficient to conclusively diagnose renal cell carcinoma.

 

Lipoma (Option D) is a benign tumour made up of fatty tissue. On imaging, it typically appears as a well-defined soft tissue mass. However, based on the X-ray image provided, a lipoma would not be the most likely diagnosis.

questions.solutionHtml:
ic type of mucus retention cyst that develops on the floor of the mouth, typically caused by blockage or rupture of the ducts of the sublingual or submandibular glands. This leads to mucus accumulation and the formation of a cystic swelling.

Ranula

Definition

Ranulas are a type of extravasation mucocele caused by the rupture of the main duct or obstructed acini of the sublingual gland. They appear as bluish swellings on the floor of the mouth and resemble the belly of a frog.

Location
  • Commonly found in the anterior floor of the mouth.
  • When it extends through the mylohyoid muscle, it presents as a submental swelling known as a "plunging ranula."

Symptoms

Typically soft, fluctuant, and painless unless infected.

Diagnosis
  • Confirmed through Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI)
  • Ultrasound
  • Aspiration of thick, sticky saliva differentiates it from a lymphangioma.

Treatment
  • Removal of the sublingual gland is preferred.
  • Incision, drainage, and marsupialisation have low success rates. Although marsupialisation is often adequate, it has a higher recurrence rate compared to sublingual gland excision.
  • OK-432 injection
  • Botulinum toxin injections

Incorrect Options:

Cystic hygroma (Option A) is a congenital abnormality of the lymphatic system, usually presenting as a soft, cystic swelling in the neck area. It is not typically found on the floor of the mouth.

Dermoid (Option C) cysts are developmental cysts that contain various tissues, such as skin, hair follicles, and sebaceous glands. While they can occur on the floor of the mouth, they are not exclusive to this region.

Branchial cysts (Option D) are congenital cysts that form from remnants of the branchial apparatus. They are primarily found in the neck area and are not commonly seen on the floor of the mouth.

questions.stem: Which of the following conditions is associated with perineural invasion?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following conditions is associated with perineural invasion?
questions.solution: ta-dictid="38c41e122116927771859b63deb0ed">cystic carcinoma Explanation: Adenoid cystic carcinoma is known for its tendency to invade along nerves (perineural invasion) , which is a key feature of its aggressive nature. Adenoid cystic carcinoma: This type of cancer primarily affects the submandibular and sublingual salivary glands, with approximately half of the cases occurring in minor salivary glands, especially in the palate. It is relatively rare in the parotid gland. Clinical features: Facial nerve palsy Pain or numbness High risk of distant metastasis, especially - lung. Histopathology of adenoid cystic carcinoma: Type: Unencapsulated, infiltrative biphasic neoplasm. Cell Types: Variable proportions of epithelial and myoepithelial cells. Patterns: Cribriform: Cells around sharply punched-out cylindromatous spaces with basophilic matrix. It is the most common type and has a better prognosis. Tubular: Bilayered tubules with a true lumen. Solid: Sheets and nests of tumour cells without a lumen. Carries poor prognosis. Nuclear Features: Small, angulated, hyperchromatic nuclei with scant cytoplasm. Perineural Invasion: Common in adenoid cystic carcinoma. High-Grade Transformation: Can occur Immunohistochemistry: Ductal cells: Positive for c-KIT. Myoepithelial cells: Positive for p63 and SMA. Incorrect Options: Pleomorphic adenoma (Option B) : This tumour generally does not show perineural invasion unless it undergoes a malignant transformation. Even in cases of malignancy, vascular invasion is more commonly seen than perineural invasion. Mucoepidermoid tumour (Option C) : While mucoepidermoid tumours can invade surrounding tissues, including nerves, perineural invasion is less common compared to adenoid cystic carcinoma. Pancreatic cancer (Option D) can invade adjacent structures and spread to distant organs, but perineural invasion is not a characteristic feature of this type of cancer. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
ta-dictid="38c41e122116927771859b63deb0ed">cystic carcinoma

Explanation:

  • Adenoid cystic carcinoma is known for its tendency to invade along nerves (perineural invasion), which is a key feature of its aggressive nature.

Adenoid cystic carcinoma:

  • This type of cancer primarily affects the submandibular and sublingual salivary glands, with approximately half of the cases occurring in minor salivary glands, especially in the palate.
  • It is relatively rare in the parotid gland.
  • Clinical features:
    • Facial nerve palsy
    • Pain or numbness
    • High risk of distant metastasis, especially - lung.

Histopathology of adenoid cystic carcinoma:

  • Type: Unencapsulated, infiltrative biphasic neoplasm.
  • Cell Types: Variable proportions of epithelial and myoepithelial cells.
  • Patterns:
    • Cribriform: Cells around sharply punched-out cylindromatous spaces with basophilic matrix. It is the most common type and has a better prognosis.
    • Tubular: Bilayered tubules with a true lumen.
    • Solid: Sheets and nests of tumour cells without a lumen. Carries poor prognosis.
  • Nuclear Features: Small, angulated, hyperchromatic nuclei with scant cytoplasm.
  • Perineural Invasion: Common in adenoid cystic carcinoma.
  • High-Grade Transformation: Can occur
  • Immunohistochemistry:
    • Ductal cells: Positive for c-KIT.
    • Myoepithelial cells: Positive for p63 and SMA.

Incorrect Options:

Pleomorphic adenoma (Option B): This tumour generally does not show perineural invasion unless it undergoes a malignant transformation. Even in cases of malignancy, vascular invasion is more commonly seen than perineural invasion.

Mucoepidermoid tumour (Option C): While mucoepidermoid tumours can invade surrounding tissues, including nerves, perineural invasion is less common compared to adenoid cystic carcinoma.

Pancreatic cancer (Option D) can invade adjacent structures and spread to distant organs, but perineural invasion is not a characteristic feature of this type of cancer.

questions.stem: What is the minimum platelet count necessary for most surgical procedures?
questions.stemHtml: What is the minimum platelet count necessary for most surgical procedures?
questions.solution: A platelet count of at least 50,000 (10^9/L) is generally considered the minimum for performing most surgical procedures safely, as it helps minimise the risk of bleeding. National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) Guidelines (2015): For invasive procedures or surgery: Platelet counts should be increased above 50,000/μL. For patients at high risk of bleeding: A platelet count of 50,000-75,000/μL is considered appropriate. For surgery at critical sites: A platelet count of > 100,000/μL is recommended. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: dfb6906b91692777189e0acce4f86">hyperdense lesion in the liver. Given the patient's clinical history of dysentery, the most likely diagnosis is an amoebic liver abscess . Amoebic liver abscess is caused by the protozoan parasite Entamoeba histolytica , typically contracted through the ingestion of contaminated food or water. On ultrasound, the abscess appears as a well-defined, hypoechoic lesion with variable internal echoes . Mild to moderate oedema in the surrounding liver parenchyma may also be seen. questions.stem: What is the primary prognostic factor that significantly influences the outcome of breast cancer?
questions.stemHtml: What is the primary prognostic factor that significantly influences the outcome of breast cancer?
questions.solution: ement of lymph nodes, particularly axillary lymph nodes , is the most important prognostic factor for breast cancer and significantly influences treatment decisions and overall survival. In breast cancer , the status of the axillary lymph nodes is the most significant prognostic factor. In metastatic breast cancer , the most important prognostic factor is the status of estrogen receptors (ER) and progesterone receptors (PR). Disease factors that influence prognosis Histologic Subtypes Invasive Ductal Carcinoma (IDC): Prognosis varies by grade and molecular markers. Invasive Lobular Carcinoma (ILC): Intermediate prognosis. Tubular and Mucinous Carcinomas: Best prognosis. Basal-like Breast Cancer: Aggressive, triple-negative, no targeted treatments. Other Subtypes: Medullary, cribriform, papillary, adenoid cystic, and metaplastic carcinomas vary in prognosis. Tumor Size & Lymph Node Pathologic staging (tumour size, lymph nodes) guides prognosis and treatment. Larger tumours and positive lymph nodes = worse prognosis Molecular Markers Hormone Receptors (ER, PR): ER-positive = better prognosis, responsive to endocrine therapy. HER-2 Status: HER-2 positive = aggressive but treatable with targeted therapies. Patient factors that influence prognosis Age Younger, particularly premenopausal women, may have higher local recurrence rates post-surgery, but radiation therapy can reduce this risk. BRCA Mutation Generally more aggressive and associated with poorer prognosis. Family History A strong family history may indicate inherited susceptibility and potentially a worse prognosis. Prior Breast Cancer History Previous breast cancer can negatively influence the prognosis of a new diagnosis. Lifestyle Factors Obesity and inactivity are linked to increased recurrence risk and may affect overall prognosis. Treatment Adherence Non-compliance can worsen prognosis. @Neet_pg_bot

ement of lymph nodes, particularly axillary lymph nodes, is the most important prognostic factor for breast cancer and significantly influences treatment decisions and overall survival.
  • In breast cancer, the status of the axillary lymph nodes is the most significant prognostic factor.
  • In metastatic breast cancer, the most important prognostic factor is the status of estrogen receptors (ER) and progesterone receptors (PR).

 

Disease factors that influence prognosis

Histologic Subtypes
  • Invasive Ductal Carcinoma (IDC): Prognosis varies by grade and molecular markers.
  • Invasive Lobular Carcinoma (ILC): Intermediate prognosis.
  • Tubular and Mucinous Carcinomas: Best prognosis.
  • Basal-like Breast Cancer: Aggressive, triple-negative, no targeted treatments.
  • Other Subtypes: Medullary, cribriform, papillary, adenoid cystic, and metaplastic carcinomas vary in prognosis.

Tumor Size & Lymph Node
  • Pathologic staging (tumour size, lymph nodes) guides prognosis and treatment.
  • Larger tumours and positive lymph nodes = worse prognosis

Molecular Markers
  • Hormone Receptors (ER, PR): ER-positive = better prognosis, responsive to endocrine therapy.
  • HER-2 Status: HER-2 positive = aggressive but treatable with targeted therapies.

Patient factors that influence prognosis

Age

Younger, particularly premenopausal women, may have higher local recurrence rates post-surgery, but radiation therapy can reduce this risk.

BRCA Mutation

Generally more aggressive and associated with poorer prognosis.

Family History

A strong family history may indicate inherited susceptibility and potentially a worse prognosis.

Prior Breast Cancer History

Previous breast cancer can negatively influence the prognosis of a new diagnosis.

Lifestyle Factors

Obesity and inactivity are linked to increased recurrence risk and may affect overall prognosis.

Treatment Adherence

Non-compliance can worsen prognosis.

questions.stem: During the examination of a patient with a hernia, a surgeon forcefully pushes the hernial sac back into the abdominal cavity without directly pushing back the contents first. What type of hernia has occurred as a result of this, which is depicted in the image below?
questions.stemHtml: During the examination of a patient with a hernia, a surgeon forcefully pushes the hernial sac back into the abdominal cavity without directly pushing back the contents first. What type of hernia has occurred as a result of this, which is depicted in the image below?
questions.solution: rong>Explanation: Reduction en masse refers to a situation where the hernia sac is forcibly pushed back into the abdominal cavity without properly reducing or returning the herniated contents to their normal position. This can occur when the hernia sac gets stuck or incarcerated within the abdominal wall opening. Reduction en masse: The condition reduction en masse is a complication associated with an inguinal hernia. In this condition, the herniated sac is inside the abdominal wall but its contents are strangulated. Clinical features: Persistent pain in the lower abdomen Localised or generalised peritonitis Absence of appreciable hernia externally Intestinal obstruction and strangulation Strangulated Hernia (Option A) : This occurs when the blood supply to the herniated contents is cut off, leading to ischemia. It is different from reduction en masse as the hernia contents remain in the hernial sac. Sliding hernia (Option C): Happens when part of the stomach slides up through the diaphragm opening (hiatus) into the chest cavity, essentially sharing a wall with the hernia sac formed by the diaphragm, causing it to protrude alongside the esophagus This is the most common type of hiatal hernia. Maydl's hernia (Option D): This is a rare hernia where two loops of bowel are within the hernial sac, with the loop between them (inside the abdomen) being at risk of strangulation. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
rong>Explanation:
  • Reduction en masse refers to a situation where the hernia sac is forcibly pushed back into the abdominal cavity without properly reducing or returning the herniated contents to their normal position.
  • This can occur when the hernia sac gets stuck or incarcerated within the abdominal wall opening.

Reduction en masse:

  • The condition reduction en masse is a complication associated with an inguinal hernia.
  • In this condition, the herniated sac is inside the abdominal wall but its contents are strangulated.
  • Clinical features:
    • Persistent pain in the lower abdomen
    • Localised or generalised peritonitis
    • Absence of appreciable hernia externally Intestinal obstruction and strangulation

Strangulated Hernia (Option A): This occurs when the blood supply to the herniated contents is cut off, leading to ischemia. It is different from reduction en masse as the hernia contents remain in the hernial sac.

Sliding hernia (Option C):

  • Happens when part of the stomach slides up through the diaphragm opening (hiatus) into the chest cavity, essentially sharing a wall with the hernia sac formed by the diaphragm, causing it to protrude alongside the esophagus
  • This is the most common type of hiatal hernia.

Maydl's hernia (Option D): This is a rare hernia where two loops of bowel are within the hernial sac, with the loop between them (inside the abdomen) being at risk of strangulation.

Anemic Hypoxia Definition : Normal PO 2 of arterial blood but inadequate hemoglobin (Hb) to carry O 2 . Causes: Anaemia (decreased Hb concentration) Carbon monoxide (CO) poisoning Altered Hb (e.g., Methemoglobin) Mechanism: Normal PO 2 : PO 2 in inspired air and arterial blood is normal. Normal Hb content, but Hb is unavailable for O 2 transport. Hb-dissociation curve shifts left, decreasing O 2 release to tissues. Incorrect Options: Hypoxic hypoxia (Option B): It is caused by low arterial PO 2 due to factors like high altitude or respiratory disease, not related to haemoglobin levels Stagnant hypoxia (Option C): It occurs due to reduced blood flow or cardiac output, causing inadequate tissue perfusion despite normal arterial PO 2 Histotoxic hypoxia (Option D): It Involves impaired cellular utilization of oxygen, often due to toxins, despite normal oxygen supply and delivery @Neet_pg_bot

omMeta" data-dictid="a249eeb5551692777189661d39c1b2">hypoxia results from insufficient or impaired hemoglobin thus leading to decreased oxygen transport and causing hypoxia.

Anemic Hypoxia

Definition: Normal PO2 of arterial blood but inadequate hemoglobin (Hb) to carry O2.

Causes:

  • Anaemia (decreased Hb concentration)
  • Carbon monoxide (CO) poisoning
  • Altered Hb (e.g., Methemoglobin)

Mechanism:

  • Normal PO2: PO2 in inspired air and arterial blood is normal.
  • Reduced O2 Transport: Inadequate Hb reduces O2 supply to tissues.
  • Mild/Moderate Anemia: Increased 2,3-DPG in red cells compensates for low Hb; severe hypoxia during exercise.
  • CO Poisoning:
    • CO binds to Hb with 210 times greater affinity than O2, forming carboxyhemoglobin (COHb).
    • Slow release of CO from COHb prevents O2 binding.
  • Normal Hb content, but Hb is unavailable for O2 transport.
  • Hb-dissociation curve shifts left, decreasing O2 release to tissues.

Incorrect Options:

Hypoxic hypoxia (Option B): It is caused by low arterial PO2 due to factors like high altitude or respiratory disease, not related to haemoglobin levels

Stagnant hypoxia (Option C): It occurs due to reduced blood flow or cardiac output, causing inadequate tissue perfusion despite normal arterial PO2

Histotoxic hypoxia (Option D): It Involves impaired cellular utilization of oxygen, often due to toxins, despite normal oxygen supply and delivery

Valsalva Maneuver

Phase I (onset of strain)

  • There is a transient increase in blood pressure that lasts for a few seconds.
  • This occurs due to increased intrathoracic pressure adding to the aortic pressure.

Phase II (phase of straining)

  • Venous return initially decreases, lowering cardiac output and blood pressure for 4 seconds.
  • Later, blood pressure returns to normal due to increased peripheral resistance from sympathetic vasoconstriction.
  • Heart rate steadily increases due to vagal withdrawal and sympathetic activation.

Phase III

  • This phase occurs following the release of strain characterized by a transient decrease in blood pressure lasting for a few seconds.
  • This is caused by the mechanical displacement of blood to the pulmonary vascular bed, which was under increased intrathoracic pressure.
  • There is little change in heart rate.

Phase IV

  • Occurs after further release of strain; blood pressure slowly increases, and heart rate decreases for about a minute.
  • This is due to an increase in venous return, stroke volume, and cardiac output.

questions.solution: Correct Answer: C - Captopril The presence of fatigue, exertional dyspnea, pedal edema, and an S3 gallop points towards heart failure. In this case, captopril (an ACE inhibitor) can be used to help prevent disease progression. Drugs to prevent the progression of heart failure: Inotropic drugs like digoxin Diuretics ACE inhibitors Angiotensin receptor blockers Beta-blockers Vasodilators like hydralazine, nitroprusside Synthetic BNP: nesiritide Neprilysin inhibitor: Sacubitril Aldosterone antagonists SGLT-2 inhibitors like dapagliflozin The first drugs patient is started on as soon as a diagnosis of Heart failure is made are: ACE inhibitors, ARBs, or ARNI (Angiotensin Receptor/Neprilysin Inhibitor). There are many contraindications to beta-blockers, so the patient is usually started on a very low dose. Verapamil (Option A) is a Calcium channel blocker, that is absolutely contraindicated in CHF. Digoxin (Option B) is incorrect as it has no role in decreasing mortality in heart failure. It only increases the force of contraction. Carvedilol (Option D) is incorrect as there are many contraindications to beta blockers, and they are not considered first line. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Answer: A) Hydrocortisone The patient's current presentation is likely due to Hypothalamic-Pituitary-Adrenal (HPA) axis suppression from abrupt discontinuation of steroids, and hydrocortisone is administered as it provides both glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid effects. Hydrocortisone , a synthetic glucocorticoid, has both glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid effects. Effects of corticosteroids on the body: Anti-inflammatory effects : It inhibits inflammatory mediators, such as prostaglandins and leukotrienes, and suppresses inflammatory cytokine production. Immunosuppressive effects : Inhibition of immune cell proliferation and function, including T-cells, B-cells, and macrophages Metabolic effects : Increased gluconeogenesis, lipolysis, and protein catabolism, leading to hyperglycemia, insulin resistance, and muscle wasting Mineralocorticoid effects : Promotion of sodium and water retention, potassium excretion, and blood pressure elevation (minimal in prednisone due to low mineralocorticoid activity). Sodium bicarbonate (Option B): has no role in the initial management of HPA axis suppression. Insulin (Option C): Glucocorticoid deficiency causes hypoglycemia; therefore treatment of choice is not insulin. Hypertonic Saline (Option D) has no role in the initial management of HPA axis suppression. @Neet_pg_bot

  • Hydrocortisone, a synthetic glucocorticoid, has both glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid effects.

Effects of corticosteroids on the body:

  • Anti-inflammatory effects: It inhibits inflammatory mediators, such as prostaglandins and leukotrienes, and suppresses inflammatory cytokine production.

  • Metabolic effects: Increased gluconeogenesis, lipolysis, and protein catabolism, leading to hyperglycemia, insulin resistance, and muscle wasting
  • Mineralocorticoid effects: Promotion of sodium and water retention, potassium excretion, and blood pressure elevation (minimal in prednisone due to low mineralocorticoid activity).

Sodium bicarbonate (Option B): has no role in the initial management of HPA axis suppression.

questions.solution: Correct Answer: A) Empagliflozin Diabetic patients with heart failure best benefit from adding a group of drugs called SGLT-2 (sodium-glucose cotransporter-2) inhibitors, and empagliflozin falls in this group. By inhibiting the SGLT-2 receptors in the proximal tubule of the kidneys, glucose (and sodium) reabsorption can be prevented. Since both sodium and glucose are osmotic molecules, increasing their excretion draws out more water, making these drugs effective in patients with heart failure. Drugs: Dapagliflozin. Empagliflozin. Correct Answer: A) Empagliflozin

Diabetic patients with heart failure best benefit from adding a group of drugs called SGLT-2 (sodium-glucose cotransporter-2) inhibitors, and empagliflozin falls in this group.

  • By inhibiting the SGLT-2 receptors in the proximal tubule of the kidneys, glucose (and sodium) reabsorption can be prevented.
  • Since both sodium and glucose are osmotic molecules, increasing their excretion draws out more water, making these drugs effective in patients with heart failure.

Drugs:

  • Dapagliflozin.
  • Empagliflozin.
  • Canagliflozin.
  • Ertugliflozin.

Linagliptin (Option B) is a dipeptidyl peptidase-4 (DPP-4) inhibitor. It is of no use in chronic heart failure.

Rosiglitazone (Option C) is a medication used in the management and treatment of type 2 diabetes mellitus. It is in the thiazolidinediones class of medications. It is of no use in chronic heart failure.

Insulin Degludec (Option D) has no use in chronic heart failure.

According to the Herrington classification, decerebrate rigidity is a form of abnormal muscle tone that occurs due to damage or dysfunction in the medulla resulting in increased activity of motoneurons that facilitate stretch reflexes.

Facilitation of stretch reflexes occurs due to two mechanisms:

  • Increased excitability of the motor neuron pool in general.
  • Increased rate of γ motor neuron discharge.

Producing a mid-collicular lesion in an experimental animal results in decerebration.

Feature

Decerebrate Rigidity

Decorticate Rigidity

Definition

A state of severe hypertonia characterized by extension of all four limbs.

A state in which the upper extremities are flexed and the lower extremities are extended.

Cause

Damage to the lower midbrain and upper pons

Damage to the upper midbrain

Mechanism

Loss of descending inhibition to the pontine reticular system causes overactivity of this system, which excites antigravity muscles.

Rubrospinal tract excitation of flexor muscles in the upper extremities results in flexion due to damage above the red nucleus.

Posture

Arms adducted and extended

Forearms pronated

Wrists and fingers flexed

Legs extended

Feet plantar flexed

Arms adducted and flexed

Wrists and fingers flexed

Legs extended

Plantar flexion of the feet

Clinical Significance

Severe brain stem damage; poor prognosis

Better prognosis than decerebrate rigidity

span> (site of the bite) is suggestive of mild to moderate Scrub Typhus in which only Doxycycline is given.

 

Scrub typhus

Causative agent 

Orientia tsutsugamushi (bacteria)

Transmission 

Chiggers (larval mites)

Vector 

Trombiculid mite (Leptotrombidium)

Geographical distribution 

Endemic in the “tsutsugamushi triangle” (parts of Asia, Australia, Pacific Islands).

Clinical manifestations

Fever, headache, muscle pain, eschar (dark, scab-like lesion at the site of bite), and lymphadenopathy.

Diagnosis 

Serological tests (ELISA, immunofluorescence) and molecular methods (PCR).

Treatment 

Antibiotics (Doxycycline, Azithromycin)

Prevention 

Avoid mite-infested areas, wearing protective clothing, and using insect repellants.

Complications 

Organ failure, acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), neurological complications.

 

Doxycycline + Azithromycin (Option B) (Dual Therapy) is given in severe scrub typhus, which presents with high-grade fever, body pain, and end-organ damage.

Ceftriaxone + Doxycycline (Option C) is not preferred in scrub typhus.

Ceftriaxone (Option D) is incorrect because Doxycycline is a preferred drug in this case.
